graph_hamilton.title: Hamiltonian graphs
graph_hamilton.summary: Hamiltonian paths and cycles visit every vertex exactly once, unlike Euler problems, which cover all edges.
graph_hamilton.definition: In a finite undirected simple graph, a Hamiltonian path is a simple path visiting every vertex exactly once. For a graph with at least 3 vertices, a Hamiltonian cycle is a simple cycle visiting every vertex exactly once before returning to its starting vertex; normally only the starting vertex is repeated at the ends of the sequence. A graph containing a Hamiltonian cycle is called Hamiltonian.
graph_hamilton.explanation: Hamiltonian problems concern vertex coverage and allow many edges to be unused. A graph with a cut vertex cannot have a Hamiltonian cycle: deleting any vertex of the cycle would leave a connected path spanning the remaining vertices. Cycles in bipartite graphs alternate between the two parts, so a Hamiltonian cycle requires the parts to have equal sizes. Dirac’s theorem gives a sufficient condition: an undirected simple graph with n≥3 and minimum degree δ≥n/2 has a Hamiltonian cycle. Failure of this condition does not imply that no such cycle exists.
notation: A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex once; a Hamiltonian cycle also returns to its starting vertex.
Dirac’s condition: n≥3 and δ(G)≥n/2 suffice for G to be Hamiltonian.
A cycle in a complete bipartite graph Kₘ,ₙ must alternate between its two vertex parts.
graph_hamilton.example: The parts of K₂,₃ are {a,b} and {x,y,z}. The path x—a—y—b—z is Hamiltonian, but the parts have different sizes, so no cycle can cover all five vertices exactly once. Thus the graph is not Hamiltonian.
common_mistakes: Thinking a Hamiltonian cycle must use every edge.
Treating a sufficient condition as necessary and using failure of Dirac’s condition to rule out Hamiltonicity.
Assuming that connectivity or an Euler circuit guarantees a Hamiltonian cycle.

graph_hamilton__spanning_paths.title: Hamiltonian paths and spanning all vertices
graph_hamilton__spanning_paths.summary: A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex once; its endpoints need not be adjacent.
graph_hamilton__spanning_paths.definition: A Hamiltonian path is a simple path containing every vertex of the graph. In an n-vertex graph it has exactly n−1 path edges. It need not use every edge of the graph.
graph_hamilton__spanning_paths.explanation: An endpoint of a Hamiltonian path may have only one incident edge, so having such a path does not guarantee a Hamiltonian cycle. Check that every step uses an actual edge and that no vertex is omitted or repeated.
notation: An n-vertex Hamiltonian path has n−1 edges.
Reversing an undirected Hamiltonian path gives another valid traversal.
graph_hamilton__spanning_paths.example: P₅ itself has a Hamiltonian path: follow the vertices in order from one end to the other.
common_mistakes: Using every edge in place of visiting every vertex.
Assuming an edge joins the endpoints to close the path.

graph_hamilton__necessary.title: Necessary conditions for a Hamiltonian cycle
graph_hamilton__necessary.summary: Connectivity, absence of cut vertices, and balanced bipartition sizes can rule out Hamiltonian cycles.
graph_hamilton__necessary.definition: An undirected simple graph containing a Hamiltonian cycle must be connected, have degree at least 2 at every vertex, and have no cut vertex. If it is bipartite, a cycle spanning all vertices requires its two parts to have equal sizes.
graph_hamilton__necessary.explanation: Deleting any vertex from a Hamiltonian cycle leaves a connected path spanning the remaining vertices, so the graph cannot have a cut vertex. A bipartite cycle must alternate between parts and therefore uses equal numbers of vertices from each. These conditions are necessary; satisfying one alone does not guarantee a cycle.
notation: A Hamiltonian graph has δ(G)≥2.
The two parts of a Hamiltonian bipartite graph have equal sizes.
graph_hamilton__necessary.example: Two triangles sharing one vertex form a connected graph with minimum degree 2. The shared vertex is a cut vertex, so the graph is not Hamiltonian.
common_mistakes: Treating a necessary condition as sufficient.
Ignoring the requirement that a bipartite cycle alternate between its parts.

graph_hamilton__dirac.title: Dirac’s sufficient degree condition
graph_hamilton__dirac.summary: Dirac’s theorem guarantees Hamiltonicity from a high minimum degree, but does not cover every Hamiltonian graph.
graph_hamilton__dirac.definition: Dirac’s theorem: an undirected simple graph with n≥3 vertices and minimum degree δ(G)≥n/2 contains a Hamiltonian cycle. Since degrees are integers, this condition is equivalent to δ≥⌈n/2⌉.
graph_hamilton__dirac.explanation: First check that the graph is simple and undirected and that n≥3. Then compute every degree and take the minimum. If the condition holds, the conclusion follows directly. If it fails, this theorem cannot decide the question; it does not rule out Hamiltonicity.
notation: δ(G)=minᵥ deg(v).
Dirac’s condition is sufficient, not necessary and sufficient.
graph_hamilton__dirac.example: C₆ has minimum degree 2, less than 6/2=3, yet it is itself a Hamiltonian cycle. Thus the condition is not necessary.
common_mistakes: Using average degree instead of minimum degree.
Declaring a graph non-Hamiltonian whenever the condition fails.

graph_hamilton__spanning_cycle.title: Hamiltonian cycles and closure
graph_hamilton__spanning_cycle.summary: A Hamiltonian cycle closes after visiting each vertex once; repeating the starting vertex at the ends is a notation convention.
graph_hamilton__spanning_cycle.definition: In an undirected simple graph with at least 3 vertices, a Hamiltonian cycle is a simple cycle spanning all vertices. In its vertex sequence, all vertices are distinct except for the common starting and ending vertex. It uses n edges.
graph_hamilton__spanning_cycle.explanation: Deleting any edge of a Hamiltonian cycle yields a Hamiltonian path. In a complete graph, every ordering of the vertices can be closed, but in a general graph each edge must be checked; an ordering alone is not enough.
notation: An n-vertex Hamiltonian cycle has n cycle edges.
When counting undirected cycles, changes of starting point and reversal are commonly regarded as the same cycle.
graph_hamilton__spanning_cycle.example: C₆ itself is a Hamiltonian cycle, whereas P₆ lacks an edge joining its endpoints and cannot be closed directly.
common_mistakes: Counting the repeated starting vertex at the end as an invalid revisit.
Listing a vertex ordering without checking the closing edge.

graph_shortest.title: Shortest paths
graph_shortest.summary: Shortest paths minimize total edge weight. Check weight signs, directions, and the reach of negative cycles before choosing an algorithm.
graph_shortest.definition: Given a weighted graph and source s, the shortest-path problem seeks the minimum traversal cost from s to each target. In a graph with nonnegative weights, repeated sections can always be removed to obtain a shortest path with no repeated vertices. The distance to an unreachable target is ∞. If a negative-cost closed walk reachable from s can also reach target t, then repeated traversal can make the s-to-t cost arbitrarily small, so no finite minimum exists.
graph_shortest.explanation: For an unweighted graph, give every edge weight 1 and use breadth-first search. Dijkstra’s algorithm repeatedly settles the unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance; its correctness requires all edge weights to be nonnegative, and zero-weight edges are allowed. Bellman–Ford handles negative edges and detects negative cycles reachable from the source. Shortest paths may be nonunique; listing all shortest simple paths requires more than one predecessor when applicable. For negative cycles, distinguish whether the cycle can reach the particular target.
notation: d(s,t) is the shortest cost from source s to target t; it is ∞ when t is unreachable.
Relax u→v: if d(u)+w(u,v)<d(v), update d(v).
Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights; a negative cycle affects a target only if it can reach that target.
graph_shortest.example: With directed edges s→a of weight 4, s→b of weight 1, b→a of weight 2, a→t of weight 1, and b→t of weight 7, the shortest path is s→b→a→t of total weight 4, better than the cost 5 via a directly.
common_mistakes: Stopping as soon as any route to the target is found.
Using Dijkstra with permanently settled vertices on a graph with negative edges without checking its applicability.
Assuming a negative cycle anywhere in the graph makes every target distance unbounded below.

graph_shortest__bfs.title: Unweighted shortest paths and breadth-first search
graph_shortest__bfs.summary: When all edges have equal cost, searching by layers gives minimum-edge distances.
graph_shortest__bfs.definition: Breadth-first search starts at the source and visits vertices in distance layers 0,1,2, and so on. In an unweighted graph, or when every edge has the same positive weight, its layer number equals the minimum number of edges from the source.
graph_shortest__bfs.explanation: A queue processes earlier layers first. On first discovering a vertex, record its distance as the previous distance plus 1 and record a predecessor. To obtain all shortest paths, keep all valid predecessors from the preceding layer rather than selecting just one.
notation: dist(s)=0; when v is first discovered from u, dist(v)=dist(u)+1.
In a directed graph, expand only along outgoing arcs.
graph_shortest__bfs.example: If s is adjacent to a and b, and both a and b connect to t, then t lies in layer 2 and can have both a and b as shortest-path predecessors.
common_mistakes: Using BFS layers as costs for arbitrary weighted graphs.
Treating the first route found by depth-first search as a shortest route.

graph_shortest__dijkstra.title: Nonnegative shortest paths and Dijkstra’s settling rule
graph_shortest__dijkstra.summary: Nonnegative edge weights allow the current smallest tentative distance to be settled safely.
graph_shortest__dijkstra.definition: Dijkstra’s algorithm maintains tentative source distances. At each step it chooses an unsettled vertex with smallest distance, settles it, and relaxes its outgoing edges. All edge weights must be nonnegative; zero-weight edges are allowed.
graph_shortest__dijkstra.explanation: Nonnegativity ensures that a detour through a more distant unsettled vertex cannot improve the current minimum. Ties may be settled in any order without changing final shortest distances, although the resulting predecessor tree may differ.
notation: Relaxation: d(v)←min(d(v),d(u)+w(u,v)).
Settle one unsettled vertex of current minimum distance at each step.
graph_shortest__dijkstra.example: For s→a of weight 4, s→b of weight 1, and b→a of weight 2, settle b first and improve a from 4 to 3. Settling a directly would miss the improvement.
common_mistakes: Applying the algorithm without modification to a graph with a negative edge.
Stopping when the target is discovered rather than correctly settled.

graph_shortest__bellman_ford.title: Negative edges and Bellman–Ford relaxation
graph_shortest__bellman_ford.summary: Negative edges can invalidate Dijkstra’s settling rule; repeated relaxation gives correct distances when no reachable negative cycle exists.
graph_shortest__bellman_ford.definition: Bellman–Ford repeatedly relaxes every arc. If no negative cycle is reachable from the source, a shortest route in an n-vertex graph can be a simple path with at most n−1 edges, so n−1 rounds suffice. A further improvement in an extra round indicates a negative cycle reachable from the source.
graph_shortest__bellman_ford.explanation: Initialize the source distance to 0 and every other distance to ∞. Relax only from tails currently reachable. A negative edge does not necessarily imply a negative cycle, so it is not a reason to reject every shortest-path problem.
notation: d(v)←min(d(v),d(u)+w(u,v)).
Negative edges are allowed, but targets without a finite shortest value must be marked separately.
graph_shortest__bellman_ford.example: For s→a of weight 1, s→b of weight 2, and b→a of weight −3, a improves from 1 to −1; its initially smaller value cannot be fixed permanently.
common_mistakes: Performing invalid numerical relaxation from an unreachable vertex at distance ∞.
Equating the existence of a negative edge with a negative cycle.

graph_shortest__negative_cycles.title: Negative cycles and affected targets
graph_shortest__negative_cycles.summary: A negative cycle reachable from the source and able to reach a target makes that target’s cost unbounded below.
graph_shortest__negative_cycles.definition: A negative cycle is a closed directed route of negative total weight. If s can reach it and it can reach t, it can be repeated arbitrarily often, making the s-to-t walk cost tend to −∞. A negative cycle unreachable from s, or a target unreachable from that cycle, is not automatically affected.
graph_shortest__negative_cycles.explanation: An unreachable target has distance ∞, which differs from a cost unbounded below. Even with a reachable negative cycle, some other targets may still have finite shortest costs; keep track of reachability to the target.
notation: Unbounded-below distance and unreachable distance ∞ are different states.
Influence chain: s⇝negative cycle⇝t.
graph_shortest__negative_cycles.example: If a negative cycle lies in a separate directed component that s cannot enter, ordinary shortest paths in the part reachable from s remain valid.
common_mistakes: Extending a negative cycle’s influence to every target in the graph.
Using ∞ to mean that cost can be decreased without limit.

graph_shortest__optimality_certificate.title: Distance potentials and shortest-path certificates
graph_shortest__optimality_certificate.summary: An edgewise potential inequality provides a lower bound on path cost; a path attaining it is optimal.
graph_shortest__optimality_certificate.definition: If h(s)=0 and every arc u→v satisfies h(v)−h(u)≤w(u,v), then h is a lower-bound potential for costs from s. Summing along any s-to-t path gives h(t)≤the path cost.
graph_shortest__optimality_certificate.explanation: A feasible path of cost exactly h(t) supplies matching, checkable lower and upper bounds and proves that the path is shortest. This verifies optimality without requiring the steps of a particular search algorithm.
notation: h(v)≤h(u)+w(u,v).
w(P)=h(t) and P feasible ⇒ P is shortest.
graph_shortest__optimality_certificate.example: With only s→a of weight 2, a→t of weight 3, and s→t of weight 7, the values h(s)=0, h(a)=2, h(t)=5 satisfy every edge constraint. The path s→a→t has cost 5 and attains the lower bound.
common_mistakes: Giving only h(t) without checking the inequality on every arc.
Claiming a path attains the bound without checking that every step exists.

graph_coloring.title: Graph coloring
graph_coloring.summary: A proper vertex coloring gives adjacent vertices different colors; the chromatic number is the least number of colors needed.
graph_coloring.definition: A proper vertex coloring of a finite undirected simple graph assigns one color to every vertex so that the endpoints of each edge have different colors. The chromatic number χ(G) is the minimum number of colors required. A bipartite graph containing an edge has chromatic number 2; a nonempty edgeless graph has chromatic number 1; the complete graph Kₙ has chromatic number n. This concerns vertex coloring, excludes loops, and does not concern edge coloring.
graph_coloring.explanation: To establish the chromatic number, first obtain a lower bound using a clique, odd cycle, or similar obstruction, then construct a coloring with that many colors for an upper bound. An undirected simple graph is two-colorable exactly when it has no odd-length simple cycle. Sequential greedy coloring follows a specified vertex order, assigning each vertex the smallest color not used by its already colored neighbors. It always produces a proper coloring with at most Δ+1 colors, but need not be optimal, and its result depends on the order.
notation: χ(G) is the chromatic number; Δ(G) is the maximum degree.
Proper coloring: uv∈E ⇒ c(u)≠c(v).
A nonempty simple graph has χ(G)≤Δ(G)+1; a bipartite graph with an edge has χ(G)=2.
graph_coloring.example: For the 6-cycle 1—2—3—4—5—6—1, color {1,3,5} with one color and {2,4,6} with another, giving chromatic number 2. A 5-cycle requires 3 colors because alternating two colors causes a conflict.
common_mistakes: Giving one k-coloring and claiming χ=k without ruling out fewer colors.
Taking the number of colors in one greedy run as the chromatic number.
Confusing vertex coloring with edge coloring, where adjacent edges must have different colors.

graph_coloring__chromatic_bounds.title: Proper vertex colorings and chromatic bounds
graph_coloring__chromatic_bounds.summary: Combine a necessary lower bound with an explicit coloring upper bound to determine the chromatic number.
graph_coloring__chromatic_bounds.definition: A proper vertex coloring gives the endpoints of every edge different colors, and χ is the least number needed. A clique of k pairwise adjacent vertices forces at least k colors; a proper k-coloring proves that at most k are needed.
graph_coloring__chromatic_bounds.explanation: Different components of a disconnected graph can reuse the same colors. Thus the graph’s chromatic number is the maximum of its component chromatic numbers, not their sum. A nonempty edgeless graph needs 1 color; a graph with an edge needs at least 2.
notation: ω(G)≤χ(G), where ω is the maximum clique size.
χ(G₁⊔G₂)=max(χ(G₁),χ(G₂)).
graph_coloring__chromatic_bounds.example: A triangle with a pendant edge still needs only 3 colors. The triangle gives the lower bound 3, and the pendant vertex can reuse a color different from its neighbor’s.
common_mistakes: Constructing a k-coloring without proving fewer colors impossible.
Adding the chromatic numbers of the components.

graph_coloring__bipartite.title: Two-coloring, bipartite graphs, and odd cycles
graph_coloring__bipartite.summary: Two-colorability is equivalent to having no odd cycle and to partitioning the vertices into two independent sets.
graph_coloring__bipartite.definition: An undirected simple graph is bipartite if its vertices can be split into two disjoint parts with every edge joining different parts. It admits a proper coloring with at most two colors exactly when it contains no odd-length simple cycle.
graph_coloring__bipartite.explanation: Colors must alternate along edges. An even cycle closes consistently; an odd cycle creates a conflict at its ends. In a graph without odd cycles, partition each component by the parity of search-tree depth. An isolated vertex may go in either part.
notation: A bipartition is V=X⊔Y, with every edge joining X to Y.
A bipartite graph with an edge has chromatic number 2; a nonempty edgeless bipartite graph has chromatic number 1.
graph_coloring__bipartite.example: C₄ can be partitioned into two sets of alternating vertices. C₃ cannot be two-colored, because its third edge would join vertices of the same color.
common_mistakes: Assuming every bipartite graph requires exactly 2 colors, ignoring edgeless graphs.
Defining bipartiteness as merely being drawable in two rows.

graph_coloring__greedy.title: Sequential greedy coloring and the maximum-degree bound
graph_coloring__greedy.summary: Greedy coloring always gives a proper coloring, but its color count depends on vertex order.
graph_coloring__greedy.definition: Sequential greedy coloring processes vertices one at a time and assigns the smallest color absent from the already colored neighbors. For a finite undirected simple graph of maximum degree Δ, any order uses at most Δ+1 colors.
graph_coloring__greedy.explanation: When a vertex is processed, it has at most Δ already colored neighbors, forbidding at most Δ colors. Thus one of the first Δ+1 colors is available. This bound does not imply that greedy coloring is always optimal or that every graph needs Δ+1 colors.
notation: χ(G)≤number of colors used by greedy coloring≤Δ(G)+1.
Vertex order may change the greedy result but cannot change the graph’s chromatic number.
graph_coloring__greedy.example: On the path a—b—c—d, processing a,d,b,c uses 3 colors, whereas processing a,b,c,d uses only 2.
common_mistakes: Treating one greedy run as the minimum chromatic number.
Assuming a new color is needed for every colored neighbor, overlooking that several neighbors may share a color.

graph_coloring__disconnected.title: Disconnected graphs and color reuse
graph_coloring__disconnected.summary: Different components have no edges between them and can share a palette instead of adding their color counts.
graph_coloring__disconnected.definition: If a nonempty finite undirected simple graph has components G₁,…,Gₖ, then χ(G)=maxᵢχ(Gᵢ). Each component supplies a lower bound; coloring them separately with the same palette supplies the upper bound.
graph_coloring__disconnected.explanation: An isolated vertex can use any existing color. A component containing an edge or clique may determine the whole graph’s chromatic number. Reusing a color in multiple components is proper because there are no edges between them.
notation: χ(G₁⊔…⊔Gₖ)=maxᵢχ(Gᵢ).
A nonempty edgeless component has chromatic number 1.
graph_coloring__disconnected.example: A disjoint triangle and a single edge have chromatic number 3, not 3+2=5.
common_mistakes: Adding the component chromatic numbers.
Assigning a distinct new color to every isolated vertex.

graph_planar.title: Planar graphs
graph_planar.summary: A planar graph can be drawn in the plane with disjoint edge interiors. Euler’s formula and edge bounds give common necessary conditions.
graph_planar.definition: A finite undirected graph is planar if it has a drawing in the plane in which the interiors of different edges do not intersect. Such a chosen drawing is a plane embedding. The regions into which it divides the plane are faces, including the unbounded outer face. A connected plane embedding satisfies n−m+f=2, where n,m,f count vertices, edges, and faces.
graph_planar.explanation: Planarity asks whether a crossing-free drawing exists; crossings in one drawing alone do not decide it. A finite undirected simple planar graph with n≥3 satisfies m≤3n−6, or m≤2n−4 if it is also bipartite. To prove the bounds, sum face boundary lengths: each edge contributes twice, once for each side. A bridge is counted twice in the boundary walk of the same face. Meeting a bound does not guarantee planarity: K₃,₃ meets the general bound but violates the bipartite bound.
notation: n=|V|, m=|E|, and f includes the outer face.
Connected plane embedding: n−m+f=2.
For n≥3, a simple planar graph has m≤3n−6; a simple bipartite planar graph has m≤2n−4.
graph_planar.example: K₄ has 4 vertices and 6 edges. Draw three vertices as a triangle, place the fourth inside, and connect it to the three corners. This gives a crossing-free drawing with 3 inner faces and 1 outer face, so 4−6+4=2.
common_mistakes: Using crossings in one drawing as proof of nonplanarity.
Omitting the outer face.
Applying 3n−6 directly to graphs with multiple edges, loops, or fewer than 3 vertices.
Treating the necessary edge bound as sufficient.

graph_planar__embedding.title: Plane embeddings and faces
graph_planar__embedding.summary: A planar graph can have different drawings. Count the outer face, and remember that a boundary may traverse a bridge twice.
graph_planar__embedding.definition: A plane embedding is a crossing-free realization of a graph in the plane. Faces are the connected regions left after removing the drawn vertices and edges. Edges may meet only at shared endpoints; a crossing without a vertex mark is not automatically a new vertex.
graph_planar__embedding.explanation: Being planar is an existence property; an embedding is a particular realization. A face boundary may be a closed walk rather than a simple cycle. If both sides of a bridge belong to the same face, the bridge contributes 2 to that face’s boundary length. The unbounded outer region is also a face.
notation: f counts all faces, including the outer face.
Face boundary length counts edge occurrences.
graph_planar__embedding.example: A path on 4 vertices has only its outer face. Its boundary walk traverses each of the 3 edges in both directions, so its length is 6, not 3.
common_mistakes: Excluding the outer face.
Counting a bridge only once in a face boundary.
Turning geometric edge crossings into vertices of the original graph.

graph_planar__euler.title: Euler’s formula and the number of faces
graph_planar__euler.summary: Vertices, edges, faces, and connected components of a plane embedding obey a unified counting formula.
graph_planar__euler.definition: A plane embedding of a finite undirected graph with n vertices, m edges, f faces, and c connected components satisfies n−m+f=1+c. For c=1 this becomes n−m+f=2. Isolated vertices count as components.
graph_planar__euler.explanation: Join distinct components with new noncrossing edges. Each such edge increases m by 1 and decreases c by 1, without changing f. Apply the connected formula, then undo the c−1 added edges to obtain the general formula.
notation: f=m−n+1+c.
Connected case: f=m−n+2.
graph_planar__euler.example: Two disjoint triangles have n=6,m=6,c=2, so f=3: two inner faces and one shared outer face.
common_mistakes: Using n−m+f=2 despite having several components.
Counting a separate outer face for each component.

graph_planar__edge_bounds.title: Planar edge bounds and proving nonplanarity
graph_planar__edge_bounds.summary: Lower bounds on face lengths yield upper bounds on edges. Violating a bound proves nonplanarity; satisfying it does not prove planarity.
graph_planar__edge_bounds.definition: For n≥3, a finite undirected simple planar graph satisfies m≤3n−6; if it is also bipartite, m≤2n−4. The first uses the face-length lower bound 3 for simple planar graphs; the second raises that bound to 4 using the absence of odd cycles in bipartite graphs.
graph_planar__edge_bounds.explanation: In the connected case, the sum of face lengths is 2m; combine this with Euler’s formula. Disconnected graphs satisfy the same bounds, but one cannot apply a formula requiring n≥3 indiscriminately to each small component. Check simplicity and vertex count before using the bounds.
notation: 3f≤2m: the face-length estimate for a simple connected plane graph.
4f≤2m: the face-length estimate for a simple connected bipartite plane graph.
graph_planar__edge_bounds.example: K₃,₃ is bipartite with n=6,m=9. If planar, it would satisfy 9≤2·6−4=8, a contradiction. Thus it is nonplanar.
common_mistakes: Applying the general edge bound to a graph with many parallel edges.
Stopping the planarity analysis after checking 3n−6.

graph_bipartite.title: Bipartite graphs
graph_bipartite.summary: A bipartite graph has two disjoint vertex parts with every edge crossing between them; equivalently, it has no odd-length cycle.
graph_bipartite.definition: A finite undirected simple graph G=(V,E) is bipartite if V is the disjoint union L∪R and each edge has one endpoint in L and one in R. Neither part may contain an internal edge, and the graph need not be connected. The complete bipartite graph Kₚ,ᵩ contains all p·q possible edges between its parts.
graph_bipartite.explanation: Starting at a vertex, alternate two colors along edges to test its component. An edge with equally colored endpoints yields an odd cycle. If every component can be two-colored, the color classes form a bipartition. Thus a finite undirected graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd cycle. Breadth-first search with adjacency lists must separately visit each unvisited component and takes O(|V|+|E|) time. Isolated vertices may go in either part.
notation: V=L⊔R means L and R are disjoint and their union is V.
Kₚ,ᵩ: the complete bipartite graph with part sizes p,q.
An odd cycle is a simple cycle with an odd number of edges.
graph_bipartite.example: For edge set {ab,ad,bc,cd,ce}, take L={a,c}, R={b,d,e}. The even cycle a−b−c−d−a does not prevent bipartiteness. Adding ac creates the triangle a−b−c−a, so the graph is no longer bipartite.
common_mistakes: Assuming the parts must have equal sizes or that every pair in different parts must be adjacent.
Assuming any cycle prevents bipartiteness, overlooking even cycles.
Coloring only one component and missing an odd cycle elsewhere.

graph_bipartite__bipartition.title: Bipartitions and complete bipartite graphs
graph_bipartite__bipartition.summary: A bipartition forbids edges within a part; only complete bipartite graphs require every possible edge between parts.
graph_bipartite__bipartition.definition: A bipartition is V=L⊔R with every edge crossing between L and R. If their sizes are p,q and every vertex of L is adjacent to every vertex of R, the graph is Kₚ,ᵩ. For positive integers p,q, it has p+q vertices and pq edges.
graph_bipartite__bipartition.explanation: The parts of a bipartite graph need not have equal sizes. In Kₚ,ᵩ each vertex of L has degree q and each vertex of R has degree p. For a general bipartite graph these are only the corresponding degree upper bounds.
notation: Kₚ,ᵩ has parts of sizes p and q.
Complete bipartite graph: m=pq.
graph_bipartite__bipartition.example: K₂,₅ has 7 vertices and 10 edges. Each vertex in the part of size 2 has degree 5; each in the other part has degree 2.
common_mistakes: Treating every bipartite graph as complete bipartite.
Assuming the parts must be equal in size.

graph_bipartite__odd_cycle.title: Odd cycles and the bipartiteness criterion
graph_bipartite__odd_cycle.summary: For a finite undirected graph, the existence of an odd-length cycle exactly determines whether a bipartition is possible.
graph_bipartite__odd_cycle.definition: An odd cycle is a simple cycle of odd length. A finite undirected simple graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle; connectivity is not required.
graph_bipartite__odd_cycle.explanation: Each edge of a bipartite graph switches parts, so a cycle returning to its starting point must have even length. Conversely, color each component by the parity of search-tree depth. An edge joining equal colors, together with the even-length tree path between its endpoints, would form an odd cycle, contradicting the assumption.
notation: Cₖ is a cycle of length k.
Cₖ is bipartite if and only if k is even.
graph_bipartite__odd_cycle.example: C₈ can be split into alternating parts. C₇ cannot: after alternating colors around the cycle, the final edge joins equal colors.
common_mistakes: Taking an even cycle as evidence of nonbipartiteness.
Checking only triangles and missing odd cycles of length 5,7, and so on.

graph_bipartite__two_coloring.title: Two-coloring and testing bipartiteness
graph_bipartite__two_coloring.summary: BFS or DFS can produce a bipartition or detect a color conflict, but must cover every component.
graph_bipartite__two_coloring.definition: A two-coloring assigns one of two colors to every vertex and requires different colors at the endpoints of every edge. Choose an unvisited vertex as a root and color it; give each newly visited neighbor the opposite color. An already colored neighbor with the current vertex’s color causes failure.
graph_bipartite__two_coloring.explanation: With adjacency lists, each vertex is processed once and each undirected edge checked at most twice, for O(n+m) time. For a disconnected graph, restart at every unvisited vertex; completing one search does not complete the whole test.
notation: color(v)∈{0,1}.
For each edge uv require color(u)≠color(v).
graph_bipartite__two_coloring.example: If a is adjacent to b,d, and both b,d are adjacent to c, color a with 0, b,d with 1, and c with 0. This gives a bipartition of the 4-cycle.
common_mistakes: Coloring only the starting component.
Recoloring one endpoint of a conflicting edge without regard to previously satisfied constraints.

graph_topological.title: Topological sorting
graph_topological.summary: A topological order lists vertices so every arc starts earlier than it ends. A finite directed graph admits such an order exactly when it has no directed cycle.
graph_topological.definition: For a finite directed graph G, a vertex sequence v₁,…,vₙ is a topological order if it lists every vertex exactly once and every arc vᵢ→vⱼ satisfies i<j. A directed graph with no directed cycle is a directed acyclic graph, or DAG. A finite directed graph has a topological order if and only if it is a DAG.
graph_topological.explanation: Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly outputs a vertex of current indegree 0 and removes its outgoing arcs. If all vertices are output, the result is a topological order. If vertices remain but no zero-indegree candidate exists, the remainder contains a directed cycle. Multiple candidates usually allow different choices. The order is unique exactly when every step has only one candidate. Topological sorting expresses precedence constraints; it does not calculate task duration or require an arc between every pair of vertices.
notation: u→v requires u to appear before v.
d⁻(v): the current indegree of v.
DAG: directed acyclic graph.
graph_topological.example: For arcs {a→c,b→c,b→d,c→e,d→e}, both a,b,c,d,e and b,d,a,c,e are topological orders. The order a,c,b,d,e is not, because b→c requires b before c.
common_mistakes: Confusing indegree 0 with outdegree 0.
Checking only consecutive entries instead of every arc.
Taking a unique initial zero-indegree vertex as proof of a unique order.
Claiming to output a complete topological order for a graph containing a directed cycle.

graph_topological__dag.title: Directed acyclic graphs and dependencies
graph_topological__dag.summary: A DAG expresses dependencies without circularity, and every directed path imposes a required order.
graph_topological__dag.definition: A finite directed graph without a directed cycle is a DAG. If u→v means u must finish before v, a valid linear schedule must put every arc forward, and hence put the start of every directed path before its end.
graph_topological__dag.explanation: Directed acyclicity does not mean the underlying undirected graph is acyclic. For example, a→b,a→c,b→c is a DAG with an underlying triangle. Adding u→v to a DAG creates a directed cycle exactly when the original graph already has a directed path from v to u.
notation: DAG: directed acyclic graph.
u⇝v: a directed path exists from u to v.
graph_topological__dag.example: The arcs {a→b,a→c,b→c} allow a,b,c. Adding c→a creates the cycle a→b→c→a.
common_mistakes: Checking only for cycles in the underlying undirected graph.
Assuming only direct arcs impose dependencies, ignoring directed paths.

graph_topological__kahn.title: The zero-indegree deletion algorithm
graph_topological__kahn.summary: Repeatedly outputting a current zero-indegree vertex constructs a topological order and detects circular dependencies.
graph_topological__kahn.definition: Kahn’s algorithm initially collects all zero-indegree vertices. Each step removes and outputs one, deletes all its outgoing arcs, and adds any vertices whose indegree has just become 0 to the candidate set. If fewer vertices are output than the graph has, it contains a directed cycle.
graph_topological__kahn.explanation: Indegrees must be updated dynamically as arcs are removed, rather than computed only initially. A queue, stack, or lexicographically smallest-candidate rule can implement the algorithm; they may yield different valid topological orders. Adjacency lists with an ordinary queue give O(n+m) time.
notation: d⁻(v): indegree in the current remaining graph.
Output count=n: a complete topological order has been obtained.
graph_topological__kahn.example: For a→c,b→c, the initial candidates are a,b. After a is taken, c still has the incoming arc from b; b must be taken before c becomes a candidate.
common_mistakes: Failing to decrease successor indegrees when a vertex is removed.
Forcing a vertex with smallest positive indegree into the output.

graph_topological__uniqueness.title: Enumerating topological orders and uniqueness
graph_topological__uniqueness.summary: Interchangeable zero-indegree candidates yield distinct orders; uniqueness requires a forced choice at every step.
graph_topological__uniqueness.definition: A DAG may have one or several topological orders. Its order is unique exactly when every step of Kahn’s deletion has exactly one zero-indegree vertex. To enumerate orders, try every current zero-indegree vertex at each step and restore the state between branches.
graph_topological__uniqueness.explanation: If a step offers distinct candidates u,v, choose u first or v first and then complete a topological order of the remaining DAG, producing at least two orders. Conversely, if every step has only one candidate, the next entry of any valid order is forced.
notation: Topological orders are distinguished by vertex labels.
Uniqueness concerns the whole deletion process, not just the first step.
graph_topological__uniqueness.example: For a→b,a→c, a must be first, but b,c can then be swapped. The two orders are a,b,c and a,c,b.
common_mistakes: Assuming a unique initial zero-indegree vertex guarantees uniqueness throughout.
Failing to restore indegrees while enumerating and losing valid branches.

graph_domination.title: Dominating sets, covers, and independent sets
graph_domination.summary: Domination concerns neighbors of vertices, vertex covers concern every edge, and independent sets forbid internal adjacency; these conditions differ.
graph_domination.definition: Let G=(V,E) be a finite undirected simple graph. A set D⊆V dominates if every vertex of V∖D is adjacent to at least one vertex of D. A vertex cover C⊆V contains at least one endpoint of every edge. An edge cover F⊆E has an incident edge at every vertex; distinguish the two covers explicitly. An independent set I⊆V has no adjacent pair of distinct vertices. Here τ means the minimum vertex-cover number.
graph_domination.explanation: Minimum dominating sets and vertex covers minimize vertex count; maximum independent sets maximize it. C is a vertex cover exactly when V∖C is independent, so τ(G)+α(G)=|V|. Dominating sets have no such complement relation. Every inclusion-maximal independent set is dominating, but can be much smaller than a maximum independent set. An isolated vertex must belong to every dominating set but need not be chosen to cover edges. A graph with an isolated vertex has no edge cover; without isolated vertices, minimum edge-cover number ρ and maximum matching number ν satisfy ρ+ν=|V|.
notation: γ(G): size of a minimum dominating set.
τ(G): size of a minimum vertex cover.
α(G): size of a maximum independent set.
N[D]=V: D together with its neighbors covers every vertex.
graph_domination.example: In the path 1−2−3−4−5, {2,4} is both a minimum dominating set of size 2 and a minimum vertex cover. The set {1,3,5} is a maximum independent set of size 3. Equality of the two minima is a feature of this example, not a general law.
common_mistakes: Equating domination of vertices with covering edges.
Confusing vertex covers with edge covers made of edges.
Reading “maximal” as “having the most vertices.”
Inferring γ=τ for every graph from one example.

graph_domination__dominating.title: Dominating sets and the domination number
graph_domination__dominating.summary: A dominating set requires each unselected vertex to neighbor a selected one; it need not cover every edge.
graph_domination__dominating.definition: In a finite undirected simple graph, D⊆V is dominating if every v∈V∖D has a neighbor in D. The minimum size is the domination number γ(G). A selected vertex does not need another selected vertex to dominate it.
graph_domination__dominating.explanation: Every isolated vertex must be selected. For maximum degree Δ, one selected vertex and its neighbors cover at most Δ+1 vertices. Thus an n-vertex graph satisfies γ(G)≥⌈n/(Δ+1)⌉. Overlap may make this bound loose, so it generally does not determine the optimum alone.
notation: N[D]=V.
graph_domination__dominating.example: In the star K₁,₄, the center alone dominates all 5 vertices, so γ=1; choosing all four leaves is unnecessary.
common_mistakes: Requiring vertices within a dominating set to be adjacent to each other.
Forgetting that a selected vertex already covers itself.

graph_domination__vertex_cover.title: Vertex covers and the vertex-cover number
graph_domination__vertex_cover.summary: A vertex cover selects at least one endpoint of every edge, unlike domination, which is defined by vertex adjacency.
graph_domination__vertex_cover.definition: In a finite undirected simple graph, C⊆V is a vertex cover if every edge has at least one endpoint in C. Its minimum possible size is τ(G). The selected objects are vertices; an edge cover instead selects edges.
graph_domination__vertex_cover.explanation: Edges of a matching share no endpoints, so covering them requires a distinct selected vertex for each edge. Every matching size is therefore a lower bound on τ(G). An isolated vertex has no incident edges to cover and need not be selected.
notation: τ(G): minimum vertex-cover size.
Every matching M satisfies |M|≤τ(G).
graph_domination__vertex_cover.example: In a triangle, selecting one vertex leaves the edge between the other two uncovered. Any two vertices cover all edges, so τ(K₃)=2.
common_mistakes: Writing an edge set as a vertex cover.
Claiming every edge is covered merely because each unselected vertex has a selected neighbor.

graph_domination__independent.title: Independent sets and the independence number
graph_domination__independent.summary: An independent set has no internal edges, and its complement is exactly a vertex cover. Distinguish maximal from maximum.
graph_domination__independent.definition: In a finite undirected simple graph, a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices is independent. A maximum independent set has the largest possible vertex count, denoted α(G). An independent set is maximal if no vertex can be added while retaining independence.
graph_domination__independent.explanation: C is a vertex cover exactly when V∖C is independent, so τ(G)+α(G)=|V|. Every maximal independent set is dominating: otherwise an outside vertex with no neighbor in the set could be added. However, different maximal independent sets can have very different sizes.
notation: α(G): maximum independent-set size.
graph_domination__independent.example: In K₁,₄, both the center alone and the set of four leaves are maximal independent sets. Only the latter is maximum.
common_mistakes: Calling every maximal independent set maximum.
Assuming an independent set cannot have edges to outside vertices.

graph_domination__edge_cover.title: Edge covers and minimum edge covers
graph_domination__edge_cover.summary: An edge cover selects edges so every vertex touches a selected edge; the selected objects differ from a vertex cover.
graph_domination__edge_cover.definition: In a finite undirected simple graph, F⊆E is an edge cover if every vertex is an endpoint of at least one edge of F. Its minimum size is ρ(G). A nonempty graph has an edge cover exactly when it has no isolated vertices. Vertex covers select vertices to cover all edges; edge covers select edges to cover all vertices.
graph_domination__edge_cover.explanation: For a finite undirected simple graph without isolated vertices, ρ(G)+ν(G)=|V|, where ν is maximum matching size. Starting from a maximum matching, add one incident edge for each unmatched vertex to construct an edge cover of size |V|−ν(G). No two unmatched vertices are adjacent, or the matching could be enlarged directly.
notation: ρ(G): number of edges in a minimum edge cover.
Without isolated vertices, ρ(G)=|V|−ν(G).
graph_domination__edge_cover.example: In 1−2−3−4−5, choose maximum matching {12,34}, then add 45 for vertex 5. The edge cover {12,34,45} has size 3. The vertex cover {2,4} has 2 vertices; these are different objects.
common_mistakes: Writing a vertex set as an edge cover.
Applying ρ=|V|−ν with isolated vertices without checking whether an edge cover exists.
Using an arbitrary maximal matching size as ν and obtaining a wrong cover number.

graph_matching.title: Graph matching
graph_matching.summary: A matching consists of edges with no shared endpoints. Augmenting paths enlarge it; in bipartite graphs Hall’s condition characterizes saturation of a specified side.
graph_matching.definition: A matching M in a finite undirected simple graph is an edge set in which distinct edges share no endpoint. A matching that cannot be enlarged by adding an edge is maximal; one with the most edges is maximum. A perfect matching has exactly one matching edge incident to every vertex. A vertex incident to no edge of M is unmatched.
graph_matching.explanation: Relative to M, an augmenting path is a simple path with both endpoints unmatched and edges alternating between nonmatching and matching edges. Flipping membership along it increases the matching size by 1. A matching in a finite graph is maximum exactly when it has no augmenting path. In a bipartite graph (L,R;E), a matching saturating all of L exists exactly when every S⊆L has |N(S)|≥|S|: Hall’s condition. Checking that individual vertices have neighbors is insufficient; subsets may share too few neighbors.
notation: ν(G): number of edges in a maximum matching.
N(S): vertices in the opposite part adjacent to at least one vertex of S.
M△E(P): flip matching membership along augmenting path P.
graph_matching.example: In 1−2−3−4, {23} is maximal since each remaining edge touches 2 or 3, but it is not maximum. The whole path is augmenting relative to it. Flipping yields {12,34}, which is also perfect.
common_mistakes: Confusing maximal and maximum matchings.
Equating saturation of the left side with covering every vertex; the two parts may differ in size.
Checking only individual degrees for Hall’s condition rather than neighbor unions of subsets.
Calling every alternating path augmenting, ignoring its unmatched endpoints.

graph_matching__maximal_maximum.title: Maximal, maximum, and perfect matchings
graph_matching__maximal_maximum.summary: Maximal concerns adding an edge, maximum compares edge counts, and perfect concerns covering every vertex.
graph_matching__maximal_maximum.definition: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. A maximal matching admits no directly added edge; a maximum matching has the largest edge count among all matchings; a perfect matching gives every vertex exactly one incident matching edge.
graph_matching__maximal_maximum.explanation: Every maximum matching is maximal, but not conversely. A perfect matching has n/2 edges and is therefore maximum. An even vertex count is only necessary for a perfect matching; isolated vertices or other obstructions may prevent one.
notation: ν(G): maximum matching size.
A perfect matching requires even n and gives ν(G)=n/2.
graph_matching__maximal_maximum.example: In a 4-vertex path, the middle edge is a maximal matching. The two end edges together are both maximum and perfect.
common_mistakes: Inferring maximum size merely because no edge can be added directly.
Assuming an even vertex count guarantees a perfect matching.

graph_matching__augmenting.title: Alternating and augmenting paths
graph_matching__augmenting.summary: An alternating path switches between matching and nonmatching edges; it directly enlarges the matching only if both endpoints are unmatched.
graph_matching__augmenting.definition: Relative to M, a path whose successive edges alternate between M and E∖M is M-alternating; it can start with either kind. If it is simple and its two distinct endpoints are unmatched by M, it is M-augmenting. Its first and last edges are nonmatching, and it has one more nonmatching edge than matching edge.
graph_matching__augmenting.explanation: Add the nonmatching edges and remove the matching edges on an augmenting path to get a matching of size |M|+1. In a finite graph, no augmenting path is equivalent to maximum size; merely having no edge that can be added directly establishes only maximality.
notation: M′=M△E(P).
After augmentation, |M′|=|M|+1.
graph_matching__augmenting.example: If a bipartite graph has M={a2} and edges b2,a1, then b−2−a−1 is augmenting. Replace a2 by b2 and a1.
common_mistakes: Ignoring that augmenting-path endpoints must be unmatched.
Adding nonmatching edges along the path without removing old ones, causing endpoint conflicts.

graph_matching__hall.title: Hall’s condition and bipartite matching
graph_matching__hall.summary: Hall’s condition asks whether every group of left vertices has enough distinct neighbors, not merely whether each vertex is nonisolated.
graph_matching__hall.definition: For a finite bipartite graph (L,R;E), a matching saturating L exists if and only if every S⊆L satisfies |N(S)|≥|S|, where N(S) is the union of the neighbors of S in R.
graph_matching__hall.explanation: Necessity follows because a matching assigns a different neighbor to every vertex of S. Sufficiency is Hall’s theorem. If |L|=|R|, saturating L gives a perfect matching of the whole graph. For unequal part sizes, say only that the left side is saturated.
notation: N(S)=⋃ᵥ∈S N(v).
Hall’s condition: ∀S⊆L, |N(S)|≥|S|.
graph_matching__hall.example: If a,b both have only neighbor 1, each has degree 1, but S={a,b} has |N(S)|=1<2. They cannot both be matched.
common_mistakes: Adding neighbor counts and counting common neighbors repeatedly.
Checking only singleton subsets.

tree_basic.title: Basic properties of trees
tree_basic.summary: A tree is a connected acyclic finite undirected simple graph. Unique simple paths, n−1 edges, and every edge being a bridge describe the same structure.
tree_basic.definition: A nonempty finite undirected simple graph is a tree if it is connected and has no cycle. An n-vertex tree has n−1 edges and exactly one simple path between any two distinct vertices. For a nonempty finite undirected simple graph, both “connected with n−1 edges” and “acyclic with n−1 edges” are equivalent to being a tree. A graph whose components are trees is a forest.
tree_basic.explanation: Connectivity guarantees reachability, and acyclicity makes simple paths unique. Removing any tree edge disconnects it. Adding a new edge between two existing distinct vertices creates exactly one cycle. A forest with n vertices and c components has n−c edges. A tree with n≥2 has at least two degree-1 vertices, called leaves. A one-vertex tree has degree 0, so leaf-counting conventions for it must be stated separately.
notation: Tree: m=n−1; forest: m=n−c.
deg(v): vertex degree in an undirected graph.
Here a leaf of a nontrivial tree means a degree-1 vertex.
tree_basic.example: For a 12-vertex tree with all degrees at most 3 and exactly three degree-3 vertices, the handshake lemma gives n₁+2n₂+9=22. Together with n₁+n₂=9, this gives 5 leaves and 4 degree-2 vertices.
common_mistakes: Inferring a tree from m=n−1 alone, omitting connectivity or acyclicity.
Treating an undirected tree as if a root had already been specified.
Using m=n−1 for a forest without counting components.
Applying “at least two degree-1 vertices” to a one-vertex tree.

tree_basic__equivalent.title: Equivalent characterizations of trees
tree_basic__equivalent.summary: Connectedness plus acyclicity, unique simple paths, or suitable combinations with n−1 edges can identify a tree.
tree_basic__equivalent.definition: For a finite undirected simple graph on n≥1 vertices, the following are equivalent: connected and acyclic; a unique simple path between every pair of distinct vertices; connected with n−1 edges; acyclic with n−1 edges.
tree_basic__equivalent.explanation: An edge count of n−1 alone is insufficient. A cyclic component and another component can together still have exactly n−1 edges. Keep the accompanying condition, such as connectivity or acyclicity, when using these characterizations.
notation: A tree has m=n−1 edges.
Every edge of a tree is a bridge.
tree_basic__equivalent.example: A disjoint triangle and a 3-vertex path have 6 vertices and 5 edges, but the graph is disconnected and cyclic, so it is not a tree.
common_mistakes: Counting edges without checking the other conditions.
Saying unique walk instead of unique simple path, overlooking walks that repeatedly go back and forth.

tree_basic__forest.title: Forests and their edge formula
tree_basic__forest.summary: Each component of a forest is a tree, so the edge formula subtracts the number of components.
tree_basic__forest.definition: An acyclic finite undirected simple graph is a forest. If it has n vertices and c components, every component is a tree and its total edge count is m=n−c. An isolated vertex is also a component.
tree_basic__forest.explanation: Summing the nᵢ−1 edges of the components gives Σ(nᵢ−1)=n−c. Removing one forest edge adds one component. A new edge joining distinct components reduces the component count by one while preserving acyclicity.
notation: m=n−c.
c=n−m.
tree_basic__forest.example: A forest with 14 vertices and 4 components has 10 edges. Add 3 edges, each joining different current components, to obtain a tree with 13 edges.
common_mistakes: Omitting isolated vertices from n or c.
Adding an edge within a component and still claiming the result is a forest.

tree_basic__degree_leaves.title: Degrees and leaves of trees
tree_basic__degree_leaves.summary: Degree sums and longest paths constrain the number of leaves; the one-vertex tree needs separate treatment.
tree_basic__degree_leaves.definition: For a finite tree with n≥2, a leaf is a degree-1 vertex. If nₖ counts vertices of degree k, then Σnₖ=n and Σk·nₖ=2(n−1), giving n₁=2+Σₖ≥₃(k−2)nₖ.
tree_basic__degree_leaves.explanation: Degree-2 vertices contribute no “leaf surplus”; each branching vertex of degree k≥3 contributes k−2. Alternatively, take a longest simple path: an extra neighbor at either endpoint would extend the path or create a cycle, so both endpoints are leaves.
notation: n₁=2+Σₖ≥₃(k−2)nₖ.
The degree sum of a tree is 2n−2.
tree_basic__degree_leaves.example: If a nontrivial tree has two degree-4 vertices and every other vertex has degree at most 2, it has 2+2·(4−2)=6 leaves.
common_mistakes: Counting degree-2 vertices along a chain as leaves.
Using n₁≥2 when n=1.

tree_rooted.title: Rooted trees
tree_rooted.summary: Choosing a root in a tree determines parents, children, depths, and subtrees; these depend on the chosen root.
tree_rooted.definition: A rooted tree is a nonempty finite undirected tree T with a specified root r. For each nonroot vertex, its parent is its neighbor on the unique simple path toward the root; its other neighbors are its children. The root has no parent. A vertex’s depth is the number of edges from the root to it; the root has depth 0. The height is the maximum depth. Here a rooted-tree leaf is a vertex with no children.
tree_rooted.explanation: The subtree at v consists of v and all its descendants. Here ancestors and descendants exclude the vertex itself. The root’s child count equals its undirected degree; a nonroot vertex’s child count is its degree minus 1. Rerooting preserves the underlying edges but may change height and the leaf set. A full m-ary tree has exactly m children at every internal vertex. With i internal vertices and l leaves, n=mi+1 and l=(m−1)i+1. These equations do not follow from an upper bound of m children alone.
notation: depth(r)=0; height is measured in edges.
children(v): the set of children of v.
Full m-ary tree: every nonleaf has exactly m children.
tree_rooted.example: For A−B−C−D−E rooted at A, height is 4 and the only rooted-tree leaf is E. Rooted at C, height is 2 and the leaves are A,E. The degree-1 vertices of the underlying undirected tree remain A,E.
common_mistakes: Counting depth from 1 without stating the convention.
Calling a nonroot vertex with one child a leaf.
Assuming a degree-1 root must be a rooted-tree leaf.
Confusing “full m-ary” with “at most m children.”

tree_rooted__hierarchy.title: Parents and ancestors in rooted trees
tree_rooted__hierarchy.summary: The unique path to the root determines the parent; ancestors and subtrees describe the full hierarchy.
tree_rooted__hierarchy.definition: In a rooted tree, the parent of a nonroot vertex is the next vertex on its unique simple path to the root. Here ancestors exclude the vertex itself, while its subtree includes the vertex and all its descendants. Children in an unordered rooted tree have no automatic left-to-right order.
tree_rooted__hierarchy.explanation: Parenthood spans only one level; ancestry may span several. Two subtrees may be disjoint or one may contain the other. Follow parent chains rather than relying on the drawing’s left and right positions.
notation: parent(v): the parent of nonroot vertex v.
Tᵥ: the subtree rooted at v containing v and its descendants.
tree_rooted__hierarchy.example: If r has children a,b and a has children c,d, then c has parent a and ancestors a,r. The subtree at a has vertices {a,c,d}.
common_mistakes: Calling every ancestor a parent.
Assigning left and right children when an ordered rooted tree has not been specified.

tree_rooted__depth_height.title: Depth, height, and rerooting
tree_rooted__depth_height.summary: Depth and height are relative to the chosen root. Rerooting may change them but preserves the underlying undirected tree.
tree_rooted__depth_height.definition: A vertex’s depth is the edge count on its unique simple path from the root; the root has depth 0. Tree height is the largest depth. The height of the subtree at v is the greatest distance from v to its descendants, which differs from v’s depth in the whole tree.
tree_rooted__depth_height.explanation: Measurements here count edges, not vertices. Rerooting can change height, parent relations, and rooted-tree leaves, while undirected distances and degrees remain unchanged.
notation: depth(r)=0.
height(T)=maxᵥ depth(v).
tree_rooted__depth_height.example: A 5-vertex path has height 4 when rooted at an endpoint and height 2 when rooted at the middle. Its underlying graph still has diameter 4.
common_mistakes: Confusing depth with subtree height.
Thinking rerooting changes undirected vertex degrees.

tree_rooted__full_mary.title: Counting full m-ary trees
tree_rooted__full_mary.summary: When every internal vertex has exactly m children, counting children gives formulas for total vertices and leaves.
tree_rooted__full_mary.definition: A rooted tree is full m-ary if every internal vertex has exactly m children. With i internal vertices, l leaves, and n total vertices, its edge count is both mi and n−1. Hence n=mi+1 and l=(m−1)i+1.
tree_rooted__full_mary.explanation: The formulas require exactly m children per internal vertex, but do not require equal leaf depths or a balanced shape. A general m-ary tree with at most m children per vertex need not satisfy the same equalities.
notation: n=mi+1.
tree_rooted__full_mary.example: A full ternary tree with 7 internal vertices has 22 total vertices and 15 leaves. Its height still depends on its actual connections.
common_mistakes: Assuming every full m-ary tree is balanced.
Using the equalities when only an upper bound of m children is known.

tree_spanning.title: Spanning trees
tree_spanning.summary: A spanning tree retains every vertex of a connected graph and selects enough edges to connect them without redundant cycles.
tree_spanning.definition: Let G=(V,E) be a nonempty finite undirected simple graph. If T=(V,F) has F⊆E and is a tree, it is a spanning tree of G. It contains every original vertex and a subset of the original edges; with |V|=n it has exactly n−1 edges. G has a spanning tree exactly when it is connected. Selecting a tree in each component of a disconnected graph gives a spanning forest.
tree_spanning.explanation: Use the edges that first discover new vertices in BFS or DFS, or repeatedly remove cycle edges from a connected graph. Every original bridge belongs to every spanning tree. Adding one nontree edge creates a unique fundamental cycle. Paths retained by a spanning tree may be long: only an unweighted BFS tree from a specified root guarantees shortest root-to-vertex paths. A spanning tree need not be induced, because an induced subgraph would keep all edges between its selected vertices.
notation: Nontree edges: E∖F.
A spanning forest has n−c edges, where c is the original component count.
tree_spanning.example: Attach a new leaf by one edge to C₆. The leaf edge is mandatory; delete exactly one of the 6 cycle edges to obtain a spanning tree. Thus the graph has 6 spanning trees.
common_mistakes: Selecting a tree while omitting original vertices.
Treating a spanning tree as an induced subgraph that must keep every original edge.
Adding every edge encountered during search and creating cycles.
Assuming every spanning tree preserves shortest paths between all pairs.

tree_spanning__construction.title: Constructing spanning trees by search
tree_spanning__construction.summary: The edges that first discover new vertices form the spanning tree, rather than all inspected edges.
tree_spanning__construction.definition: In a finite connected undirected graph, run BFS or DFS from any root. On first visiting each nonroot vertex, record one parent edge from a visited vertex. These n−1 parent edges connect all vertices without cycles and form a spanning tree.
tree_spanning__construction.explanation: BFS discovers vertices by unweighted distance layers, so its root-to-vertex tree distances equal original shortest distances. DFS explores deeply and does not guarantee this property. In a disconnected graph, restarting searches produces only a spanning forest.
notation: Record one parent edge for each nonroot vertex.
BFS and DFS with adjacency lists both take O(n+m).
tree_spanning__construction.example: In a triangle, BFS from a records ab,ac and completes a spanning tree. Inspecting bc later must not add it as a parent edge.
common_mistakes: Recording every encountered edge as a tree edge.
Assuming a DFS tree must be a shortest-path tree.

tree_spanning__exchange.title: Fundamental cycles and tree-edge exchanges
tree_spanning__exchange.summary: A nontree edge and the unique tree path between its endpoints form one cycle; removing another edge of that cycle gives a new spanning tree.
tree_spanning__exchange.definition: Let T be a spanning tree of G and e=uv a nontree edge. The unique u-to-v simple path in T together with e is its fundamental cycle. Removing any tree edge of this cycle other than e gives another spanning tree of G.
tree_spanning__exchange.explanation: There is just one cycle after adding e: T was acyclic and its u-to-v path was unique. Removing a cycle edge preserves connectivity and restores n−1 edges. Removing a tree edge outside the cycle can instead disconnect the graph while leaving the cycle.
notation: Cₑ=P_T(u,v)∪{e}.
T′=T+e−f, where f∈Cₑ∖{e}.
tree_spanning__exchange.example: Adding ad to a−b−c−d forms a−b−c−d−a. Remove bc to leave ab,ad,cd, still a spanning tree.
common_mistakes: Assuming any tree edge can be deleted after adding a nontree edge.
Forgetting uniqueness of the original tree path.

tree_spanning__bridge_count.title: Bridge decomposition and spanning-tree counts
tree_spanning__bridge_count.summary: Bridges are mandatory in every spanning tree; independent parts joined by bridges have multiplicative tree counts.
tree_spanning__bridge_count.definition: An edge of a connected graph is a bridge if deleting it disconnects the graph. Every spanning tree contains every bridge. If disjoint connected graphs G₁,G₂ are joined by one new bridge, the resulting graph has τ(G₁)τ(G₂) spanning trees.
tree_spanning__bridge_count.explanation: Once the mandatory bridge is fixed, choose spanning trees on the two sides independently. No cycle can cross between them, so the multiplication rule applies. A single cycle Cₖ has k spanning trees, because exactly one cycle edge must be removed.
notation: τ(G₁—bridge—G₂)=τ(G₁)τ(G₂).
τ(Cₖ)=k, k≥3.
tree_spanning__bridge_count.example: Join a triangle and a 4-cycle by one bridge. Include the bridge and choose independently among 3 and 4 trees, giving 12 spanning trees.
common_mistakes: Treating a bridge as optional.
Forgetting to include the connecting bridge after choosing trees on both sides.

tree_mst.title: Minimum spanning trees
tree_mst.summary: A minimum spanning tree minimizes total edge weight among all spanning trees; its objective differs from that of a shortest-path tree.
tree_mst.definition: Let G be a nonempty finite connected undirected simple graph, with a real weight w(e) on every edge. A spanning tree T minimizing Σₑ∈T w(e) among all spanning trees is a minimum spanning tree. Weights may repeat, be zero, or be negative. A disconnected graph has no spanning tree of the whole graph; instead consider a minimum spanning forest of its components.
tree_mst.explanation: Kruskal considers edges in increasing weight order and adds those that do not create cycles. Prim grows a vertex set by repeatedly taking a lightest edge crossing its current cut. A unique lightest cut edge belongs to every MST; a unique heaviest cycle edge belongs to no MST. Distinct edge weights guarantee uniqueness but are not necessary for it. An MST minimizes total weight, not each individual source-to-vertex path.
notation: w(T)=Σₑ∈T w(e): total spanning-tree weight.
Cut δ(S): edges with one endpoint in a nonempty proper subset S and the other in V∖S.
MST: minimum spanning tree.
tree_mst.example: For triangle weights w(ab)=−3,w(ac)=1,w(bc)=4, any two edges form a spanning tree. Their total weights are −2,1,5, so {ab,ac} is an MST. Negative edges do not invalidate this finite optimization problem.
common_mistakes: Confusing an MST with a shortest-path tree from a source.
Assuming negative edges prevent Kruskal or Prim.
Inferring nonuniqueness merely from repeated weights.
Claiming a tied lightest edge must occur in every MST.

tree_mst__greedy.title: Kruskal’s and Prim’s algorithms
tree_mst__greedy.summary: Kruskal chooses safe edges from globally light edges; Prim chooses a lightest cut edge out of its current connected vertex set.
tree_mst__greedy.definition: Kruskal processes edges in nondecreasing weight order, adding an edge only if it creates no cycle, until n−1 edges have been chosen. Prim starts at one vertex and repeatedly takes a lightest edge joining the chosen vertex set to an outside vertex, adding that vertex. Both apply to finite connected undirected graphs with real edge weights.
tree_mst__greedy.explanation: Kruskal often uses a disjoint-set structure to check whether endpoints are already connected. Prim maintains candidate edges of the current cut. Negative weights are allowed, and ties may be broken arbitrarily. Different tie choices can give different MSTs with the same total weight.
notation: Kruskal: choose a lightest edge that does not create a cycle.
Prim: choose a lightest edge of the current cut.
tree_mst__greedy.example: For triangle weights ab=1,bc=2,ac=7, Kruskal chooses ab,bc. Prim from c first chooses cb, then ba, giving the same result.
common_mistakes: Ignoring Kruskal’s cycle condition.
Restricting Prim’s candidates to edges from only the most recently added vertex.

tree_mst__cut.title: The cut property and safe edges
tree_mst__cut.summary: A lightest cut edge can extend an appropriate optimum safely; if uniquely lightest, it is mandatory in every optimum tree.
tree_mst__cut.definition: For a nonempty proper S⊂V, δ(S) is the set of edges crossing between S and V∖S. A unique lightest edge of this cut belongs to every MST. If several edges tie for lightest, a specified one belongs to at least one MST, but need not belong to every MST.
tree_mst__cut.explanation: Use an exchange proof: add the edge to an optimal tree omitting it, creating a cycle that contains another cut-crossing edge. Replacing that edge by the light edge does not increase total weight. If uniquely lightest, it strictly decreases weight, yielding a contradiction; this proves the required safety or necessity.
notation: δ(S): the cut between S and its complement.
Uniquely lightest: w(e)<w(f) for every other f∈δ(S).
tree_mst__cut.example: If the edges incident to d have weights 2,5,8, the weight-2 edge is uniquely lightest in δ({d}) and belongs to every MST.
common_mistakes: Replacing “some optimum contains it” with “every optimum contains it.”
Comparing edges without restricting them to the same cut.

tree_mst__uniqueness.title: MST uniqueness and the cycle property
tree_mst__uniqueness.summary: Distinct weights ensure uniqueness, and a strictly heaviest cycle edge is excluded. Tied weights require further analysis.
tree_mst__uniqueness.definition: In a finite connected weighted graph, distinct edge weights imply a unique MST. If an edge is strictly heavier than every other edge of a cycle, it belongs to no MST. Without strictness, the same exclusion does not follow.
tree_mst__uniqueness.explanation: The cycle property follows by exchange. If an optimal tree contains the unique heaviest edge, delete it to form a cut. Another, lighter edge of the original cycle crosses that cut and can replace it, reducing weight. Equal weights need not cause multiple optima: a triangle weighted 1,1,2 still has a unique MST.
notation: A unique heaviest cycle edge belongs to no MST.
Distinct weights are a sufficient condition for uniqueness.
tree_mst__uniqueness.example: A triangle with all weights 1 has 3 MSTs. With weights 1,1,2, only the two weight-1 edges can be chosen, so the MST is unique.
common_mistakes: Treating distinct weights as necessary for uniqueness.
Excluding all tied heaviest edges from every optimum tree.

tree_matrix_tree.title: The matrix-tree theorem
tree_matrix_tree.summary: The matrix-tree theorem converts spanning-tree counting into a determinant of a principal Laplacian minor.
tree_matrix_tree.definition: Let G be a finite undirected simple graph with vertices ordered v₁,…,vₙ. Let A be its adjacency matrix and D its diagonal degree matrix. Its Laplacian is L=D−A: Lᵢᵢ=deg(vᵢ), distinct adjacent vertices give entries −1, and other entries are 0. Deleting row i and column i gives L⁽ⁱ⁾. The matrix-tree theorem states det L⁽ⁱ⁾=τ(G), the number of spanning trees.
tree_matrix_tree.explanation: Deleting the same-index row and column gives a principal minor with no additional sign. Every choice of i gives the same value. Since every row sum of L is 0, det L=0, so the full determinant cannot replace the principal minor. For n≥2, these minors vanish for a disconnected graph. A single-vertex graph has 1 spanning tree, corresponding to the 0×0 determinant convention 1. With edge variables in a weighted Laplacian, the cofactor instead gives the sum of products of edge weights over all spanning trees, not directly the MST weight.
notation: L=D−A: Laplacian of an undirected simple graph.
L⁽ⁱ⁾: delete row i and column i.
τ(G)=det L⁽ⁱ⁾; the full matrix has det L=0.
tree_matrix_tree.example: For K₃, L=[[2,−1,−1],[−1,2,−1],[−1,−1,2]]. Delete the last row and column to obtain [[2,−1],[−1,2]], with determinant 4−1=3. These are exactly the 3 spanning trees obtained by deleting any one of the three edges.
common_mistakes: Using the full Laplacian determinant and wrongly concluding a connected graph has no spanning tree.
Putting vertex numbers or 1 on the diagonal instead of degrees.
Deleting differently indexed rows and columns and ignoring the sign needed for nonprincipal minors.
Confusing the number of spanning trees with MST total weight.

tree_matrix_tree__laplacian.title: The Laplacian matrix of an undirected graph
tree_matrix_tree__laplacian.summary: The Laplacian records degrees on its diagonal and negatives of adjacencies off the diagonal.
tree_matrix_tree__laplacian.definition: For a finite undirected simple graph with ordered vertices, let A be the adjacency matrix and D the diagonal degree matrix. The Laplacian is L=D−A. It is symmetric, with all row and column sums 0, so the full determinant of a nonempty graph is 0.
tree_matrix_tree__laplacian.explanation: Relabeling vertices simultaneously permutes rows and columns and does not change graph-counting properties. An isolated vertex gives a zero row and column. When reordering, do not swap only rows without the corresponding columns.
notation: Lᵢᵢ=deg(vᵢ).
For i≠j, Lᵢⱼ is −1 or 0.
tree_matrix_tree__laplacian.example: For a−b−c ordered a,b,c, L=[[1,−1,0],[−1,2,−1],[0,−1,1]], whose rows all sum to 0.
common_mistakes: Putting +1 in adjacent off-diagonal entries.
Setting every diagonal entry to 1.

tree_matrix_tree__cofactor.title: Principal cofactors and spanning-tree counts
tree_matrix_tree__cofactor.summary: Deleting a row and column with the same index gives a determinant equal to the tree count, independent of the index.
tree_matrix_tree__cofactor.definition: For a finite undirected simple graph, let L⁽ⁱ⁾ be the principal submatrix obtained by deleting row i and column i from its Laplacian. The matrix-tree theorem gives τ(G)=det L⁽ⁱ⁾. For one vertex, use the convention that the empty determinant is 1.
tree_matrix_tree__cofactor.explanation: The full determinant det L=0 does not give the tree count. Deleting different row and column indices may produce a signed ordinary minor; the cofactor includes the extra factor (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲ. Principal cofactors are the most direct way to count and avoid this sign ambiguity.
notation: τ(G)=det L⁽ⁱ⁾.
Cofactor Cᵢⱼ=(−1)ⁱ⁺ʲ det(the matrix obtained from L by deleting row i and column j).
tree_matrix_tree__cofactor.example: For K₂, L=[[1,−1],[−1,1]], and a principal minor is 1. But deleting row 1 and column 2 gives the ordinary minor −1, so the sign matters.
common_mistakes: Using the full det L instead of a cofactor.
Treating every nonprincipal minor directly as a nonnegative tree count.

tree_matrix_tree__decomposition.title: Decomposing spanning-tree counts
tree_matrix_tree__decomposition.summary: Choosing a cofactor at a suitable cut vertex or leaf can split a large determinant into smaller blocks.
tree_matrix_tree__decomposition.definition: Suppose connected G consists of connected subgraphs G₁,G₂ sharing only one vertex v, with no other edges between the blocks. Then τ(G)=τ(G₁)τ(G₂). Deleting v’s row and column from the Laplacian yields a block diagonal matrix of the two corresponding principal minors.
tree_matrix_tree__decomposition.explanation: A bijection choosing one spanning tree on each side gives the same decomposition. Adding a new leaf leaves the tree count unchanged because its edge is mandatory. Deleting the attachment vertex’s row and column adds just a diagonal block of value 1 to the new cofactor. Check that no extra edges join the blocks before applying the decomposition.
notation: det diag(B₁,B₂)=det(B₁)det(B₂).
Adding a new leaf preserves τ.
tree_matrix_tree__decomposition.example: For two triangles sharing exactly one vertex, delete that vertex’s row and column to get two [[2,−1],[−1,2]] blocks. The tree count is 3·3=9.
common_mistakes: Multiplying directly when the subgraphs share an edge or have additional edges between them.
Thinking that choosing the block trees independently also requires choosing the shared vertex.

algebra_system.title: Algebraic systems
algebra_system.summary: An algebraic system studies a nonempty set together with specified operations on it.
algebra_system.definition: An algebraic system consists of a nonempty underlying set with specified operations. A binary operation is a function A×A→A, so every input pair must have a unique output in A. Associativity, commutativity, and identity elements are possible properties, not automatic requirements satisfied by every binary operation.
algebra_system.explanation: The same set with different operations gives different systems. First check that the rule is everywhere defined and closed, then examine properties such as associativity. A finite set can be described by a complete operation table. Failure in one row or one triple is enough to refute the corresponding universal property.
notation: (A,*) means set A equipped with binary operation *.
Associativity: (a*b)*c=a*(b*c).
A two-sided identity e satisfies e*a=a*e=a.
algebra_system.example: On the integers, define a*b=a+b+2. Then (a*b)*c=a+b+c+4=a*(b*c), and the identity is −2. Although this is not ordinary addition, its algebraic properties can be checked directly.
common_mistakes: Checking only a few examples and declaring associativity for all elements.
Calling a rule with outputs outside the set a binary operation on that set.
Confusing left, right, and two-sided identities.

algebra_system__associativity.title: Associativity of a binary operation
algebra_system__associativity.summary: Associativity determines whether parentheses can be omitted in repeated operations.
algebra_system__associativity.definition: An operation * on A is associative if (a*b)*c=a*(b*c) for all a,b,c∈A. This changes only the parentheses, not the order of the elements.
algebra_system__associativity.explanation: Prove it by expanding for arbitrary elements or using a known associative rule. One triple suffices to refute it. Associativity is essential to semigroups and groups but is not automatic for binary operations.
notation: Associativity involves three arbitrary elements.
algebra_system__associativity.example: For integer subtraction with 4,2,1, the left association gives 1 and the right gives 3, so subtraction is not associative.
common_mistakes: Confusing changing parentheses with swapping factors.
Using a few successful examples to prove a statement about all triples.

algebra_system__binary_operations.title: Binary operations and closure
algebra_system__binary_operations.summary: A binary operation must give every pair of elements a unique output still in the underlying set.
algebra_system__binary_operations.definition: A binary operation on a nonempty set A is a function *:A×A→A. Its rule must be defined on every ordered pair from A, with output in A. For a finite set, an operation table can list every case.
algebra_system__binary_operations.explanation: Only a closed, defined rule can be considered for associativity or identity elements. An output outside A, or an undefined input such as division by 0, means the rule is not a binary operation on A.
notation: Every operation-table entry must contain one element of A.
algebra_system__binary_operations.example: On {0,1,2}, both (a+b) mod3 and max(a,b) are closed. Ordinary integer addition is not, since 2+2=4 lies outside the set.
common_mistakes: Checking only some input pairs.
Mistaking “the result is a number” for closure in the specified set.

algebra_system__commutativity.title: Commutativity of a binary operation
algebra_system__commutativity.summary: Commutativity requires the output to stay unchanged when the two inputs are swapped.
algebra_system__commutativity.definition: An operation * on A is commutative if a*b=b*a for all a,b∈A. Commutativity and associativity are different properties and cannot replace each other.
algebra_system__commutativity.explanation: A finite operation table is commutative exactly when it is symmetric about the main diagonal. On infinite sets, a general verification is usually needed. A group need not be commutative; a commutative group is called abelian.
notation: a*b=b*a.
A finite operation table is symmetric about the main diagonal.
algebra_system__commutativity.example: Since max(a,b)=max(b,a), maximum is commutative. Integer subtraction is not: 4−2≠2−4.
common_mistakes: Inferring commutativity from associativity.
Checking only a=b, which cannot reveal any difference on swapping inputs.
