q_graph_shortest_08.explanation: The local edge inequalities give a global lower bound on all path costs, and the explicit path gives an upper bound attaining it. Their equality is a directly checkable optimality certificate.
q_graph_shortest_08.grading_criteria: Write edge inequalities for an arbitrary path: 30%; telescope to a lower bound: 40%; use P’s equality to prove optimality: 30%.

q_graph_coloring_05.title: Reusing colors in a disconnected graph
q_graph_coloring_05.statement: An undirected simple graph is the disjoint union of triangle abc, edge de, and isolated vertex f. Find its chromatic number and an optimal coloring.
q_graph_coloring_05.answer_text: The chromatic number is 3. One coloring is a=1,b=2,c=3,d=1,e=2,f=1.
q_graph_coloring_05.explanation: The triangle forces at least 3 colors. Components have no edges between them and may reuse colors. The given proper coloring uses just 3; the edge and isolated vertex need no new colors.
q_graph_coloring_05.grading_criteria: Triangle lower bound: 30%; proper coloring reusing colors: 50%; conclude 3: 20%.

q_graph_coloring_06.title: The Δ+1 bound for greedy coloring
q_graph_coloring_06.statement: Prove that for a finite undirected simple graph of maximum degree Δ, greedy coloring in any vertex order, choosing the smallest available positive integer color, uses at most Δ+1 colors.
q_graph_coloring_06.answer_text: When any vertex v is processed, at most deg(v)≤Δ neighbors are already colored, so they use at most Δ distinct colors. At least one color among 1,…,Δ+1 is absent from them. Greedy’s smallest available color is therefore at most Δ+1. This holds at every step, so the total is at most Δ+1.
q_graph_coloring_06.explanation: The proof gives an algorithmic upper bound, not a promise to use exactly Δ+1 or to attain the chromatic number. Later vertices avoid earlier neighbor colors, so the final coloring is proper.
q_graph_coloring_06.grading_criteria: At most Δ forbidden colors: 45%; an available color among Δ+1: 40%; applicability at every step in any order: 15%.

q_graph_coloring_07.title: Modeling scheduling conflicts as coloring
q_graph_coloring_07.statement: Activities a,b,c,d conflict in exactly the pairs ab,bc,ca,cd. Conflicting activities cannot share a time slot; other activities may run together. Ignoring space and attendance limits, what is the fewest slots? Give a schedule and prove minimality.
q_graph_coloring_07.answer_text: At least and exactly 3 slots are needed. Use slot 1 for a,d, slot 2 for b, and slot 3 for c.
q_graph_coloring_07.explanation: Model activities as vertices, conflicts as undirected edges, and slots as colors. Since a,b,c pairwise conflict, at least 3 slots are necessary. Activity d conflicts only with c and can share a’s slot, so the schedule attains the bound.
q_graph_coloring_07.grading_criteria: Correct model or explanation of conflicts and different colors: 25%; triangle lower bound: 30%; valid 3-slot schedule: 45%.

q_graph_coloring_08.title: Chromatic-number change after adding an edge
q_graph_coloring_08.statement: Let G be a nonempty finite undirected simple graph with nonadjacent u,v, and let H be obtained by adding uv. Prove χ(G)≤χ(H)≤χ(G)+1.
q_graph_coloring_08.answer_text: Any proper coloring of H remains proper for G after uv is deleted, so χ(G)≤χ(H). Take an optimal χ(G)-coloring of G. If u,v have different colors, it already colors H properly. If they share a color, give only u a completely new color. Every old edge stays proper and uv now has different colors, so H needs at most χ(G)+1 colors.
q_graph_coloring_08.explanation: Adding a constraint cannot decrease the minimum color count. Giving one endpoint a new color handles the added constraint with at most one extra color. Both equality cases are possible; the count need not increase by 1.
q_graph_coloring_08.grading_criteria: Lower bound via deleting the edge: 35%; distinguish equal and different endpoint colors: 25%; construct at most one new color and verify validity: 40%.

q_graph_connectivity_09.title: Distinguishing walks, trails, paths, and cycles
q_graph_connectivity_09.statement: An undirected simple graph has only ab,bc,ca,cd. For P=a—b—c—d, Q=a—b—c—a, and R=a—b—a—c, determine whether each is a trail, simple path, and simple cycle. Are all three walks?
q_graph_connectivity_09.answer_text: All are walks. P is a trail and simple path, but not a simple cycle. Q is a closed trail and simple cycle, but not a simple path. R repeats undirected edge ab, so it is neither a trail nor a simple path nor a simple cycle.
q_graph_connectivity_09.explanation: P repeats no vertex or edge. Q repeats a only at its ends and goes once around the triangle with distinct edges, meeting the simple-cycle convention but not distinct-vertex path convention. In R, ab and ba are the same undirected edge, so it is not a trail; it also repeats a and has different endpoints.
q_graph_connectivity_09.grading_criteria: All three are walks: 10%; P classification: 25%; Q classification: 30%; R classification and explanation that reversal uses the same edge: 35%.

q_graph_planar_01.title: Finding faces from vertex and edge counts
q_graph_planar_01.statement: A connected undirected simple graph is drawn in the plane without crossings, with 7 vertices and 10 edges. Including the outer face, how many faces are there?
q_graph_planar_01.explanation: This is a connected plane embedding. Euler’s formula gives f=2−n+m=2−7+10=5. The outer face is already among the 5 and must not be added again.
q_graph_planar_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for C. Adding the outer face once more is double counting.

q_graph_planar_02.title: Bipartite edge counts and planarity
q_graph_planar_02.statement: A connected undirected simple bipartite graph has 9 vertices and 15 edges. Can it have a crossing-free plane embedding? Explain using a necessary edge-count condition.
q_graph_planar_02.answer_text: No. If planar, since n=9≥3 and the graph is simple and bipartite, it would satisfy m≤2n−4=14. But m=15>14, a contradiction. Thus it is nonplanar.
q_graph_planar_02.explanation: Bipartite graphs have no odd cycles, allowing face-length bound 4 rather than 3 and a stronger edge bound than for general planar graphs. Checking only 15≤3·9−6 does not settle this problem.
q_graph_planar_02.grading_criteria: Applicable assumptions and m≤2n−4: 40%; substitute to obtain 14: 30%; conclude nonplanarity: 30%.

q_graph_planar_03.title: Planarity versus a particular drawing
q_graph_planar_03.statement: Which statements about planarity of finite undirected simple graphs are correct?
q_graph_planar_03.explanation: A is false: K₃,₃ has 6 vertices and 9 edges, satisfying 9≤12, but is nonplanar. B is true: a crossing drawing does not exclude a different crossing-free drawing. C is true: use a triangle as the outer boundary and one interior vertex for K₄. D is true: restricting a plane embedding to a subgraph preserves absence of crossings, but K₅ violates m≤3n−6. Thus any graph containing K₅ as a subgraph is nonplanar.
q_graph_planar_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for exactly B,C,D. When scoring reasoning, credit each judgment and justification as appropriate; selecting A precludes full credit.

options.text: If n≥3 and m≤3n−6, the graph must be planar.
Crossings in a particular drawing do not suffice to prove the original graph nonplanar.
The complete graph K₄ has a plane embedding.
A graph containing K₅ as a subgraph must be nonplanar.

q_graph_planar_04.title: Proving K₃,₃ nonplanar using face lengths
q_graph_planar_04.statement: Without directly citing the conclusion that K₃,₃ is nonplanar, use Euler’s formula and face-length counting to prove it has no plane embedding.
q_graph_planar_04.answer_text: Suppose K₃,₃ has a plane embedding. It is connected with n=6,m=9, so Euler’s formula gives f=2−6+9=5. It is simple and bipartite and hence has no triangles. Every edge belongs to a 4-cycle, so none is a bridge. Therefore every face boundary has length at least 4. Face lengths sum to 2m=18, so 4f≤18, that is, 20≤18, a contradiction. Thus K₃,₃ has no plane embedding.
q_graph_planar_04.explanation: The contradiction uses connectivity, simplicity, and bipartiteness together. Seeing crossings in a drawing is not a proof of nonplanarity.
q_graph_planar_04.grading_criteria: State n,m and assume a plane embedding: 20%; use Euler’s formula for f: 25%; justify face length at least 4 and 4f≤2m: 35%; contradiction and conclusion: 20%.

q_graph_planar_05.title: A tree’s faces and bridge boundary counts
q_graph_planar_05.statement: An undirected simple tree with 5 vertices has a plane embedding. It has ____ faces. Counting edge occurrences in a boundary walk, the unique face has total boundary length ____.
q_graph_planar_05.answer_text: There is 1 face, of boundary length 8.
q_graph_planar_05.explanation: The tree has 4 edges. Euler’s formula gives f=2−5+4=1. Each tree edge is a bridge and occurs twice in the unique face’s boundary walk, giving length 2·4=8.
q_graph_planar_05.grading_criteria: Face count 1: 40%; boundary length 8 with the reason that bridges count twice: 60%.

q_graph_planar_06.title: Faces in a disconnected embedding
q_graph_planar_06.statement: The plane contains two disjoint triangles and an isolated vertex, with no other edges. (1) How many faces are there? (2) Draw a new noncrossing edge from the isolated vertex to a vertex of one triangle. Does the number of faces change?
q_graph_planar_06.answer_text: (1) n=7,m=6,c=3, so f=m−n+1+c=6−7+1+3=3. (2) The new edge joins different components. Now m=7,c=2,n=7, so f=7−7+1+2=3, unchanged.
q_graph_planar_06.explanation: Each triangle encloses an inner face, and the graph has just one shared outer face. A new bridge connecting components does not enclose a new face.
q_graph_planar_06.grading_criteria: Count the isolated vertex and all three components: 30%; first face count: 30%; explain changes in edges and components and conclude the second part: 40%.

q_graph_planar_07.title: Face lengths at the bipartite planar edge bound
q_graph_planar_07.statement: A connected undirected simple bipartite graph has 8 vertices,12 edges, and a given plane embedding. Find the face count and decide whether every face boundary must have length 4. Count multiplicities in boundary walks.
q_graph_planar_07.answer_text: Euler’s formula gives f=2−8+12=6. Each face of this simple bipartite plane graph has length at least 4. Their lengths sum to 2m=24=4f, so every face boundary has length 4.
q_graph_planar_07.explanation: If any face had length greater than 4 while all others had length at least 4, the sum would exceed 24. “Every face” includes the outer face.
q_graph_planar_07.grading_criteria: Find 6 faces: 30%; each face length at least 4 and total 24: 40%; use equality to prove all lengths are 4: 30%.

q_graph_planar_08.title: Diagnosing a check of only the general edge bound
q_graph_planar_08.statement: Someone says: “K₃,₃ has 6 vertices and 9 edges, and 9≤3·6−6, so it is planar.” Identify the error and give a correct nonplanarity test.
q_graph_planar_08.answer_text: The error is treating a necessary planar edge bound as sufficient. The inequality m≤3n−6 does not guarantee planarity. Since K₃,₃ is simple and bipartite, planarity would also require m≤2n−4=8. It has 9 edges, violating this necessary condition, so it is nonplanar.
q_graph_planar_08.explanation: The general edge bound does not rule out every nonplanar graph. Use the stronger necessary condition supplied by the bipartite structure.
q_graph_planar_08.grading_criteria: Identify confusion of necessity and sufficiency: 40%; use bipartiteness and compute bound 8: 40%; conclude nonplanarity: 20%.

q_graph_bipartite_01.title: Recognizing bipartite graphs using odd cycles
q_graph_bipartite_01.statement: Which finite undirected simple graph below is not bipartite? Cₖ denotes a cycle of length k and K₁,₅ a star with 5 leaves.
q_graph_bipartite_01.explanation: C₆ admits alternating two-coloring. A star is a tree and can be partitioned by parity of distance from its center. K₂,₃ is bipartite by definition. C₇ is an odd cycle and cannot be two-colored, so it is not bipartite.

options.text: C₆
K₁,₅
K₂,₃
C₇

q_graph_bipartite_02.title: Obtaining a bipartition from search
q_graph_bipartite_02.statement: An undirected simple graph has vertices {a,b,c,d,e,f,g} and edges {ab,ad,bc,cd,ce,ef,fg}, where xy means {x,y}. Starting from a, color by distance parity, give a bipartition, and check that every edge crosses parts.
q_graph_bipartite_02.answer_text: Take L={a,c,f}, R={b,d,e,g}. Edges ab,ad join a to b,d; bc,cd join c to b,d; ce joins c to e; ef joins e to f; fg joins f to g. Every edge crosses L,R, so the bipartition is valid.
q_graph_bipartite_02.explanation: Distances from a are 0 at a, 1 at b,d, 2 at c, 3 at e, 4 at f, and 5 at g. Group by even and odd distance. Swapping the two parts is equally correct.
q_graph_bipartite_02.grading_criteria: Complete disjoint partition: 50%; check all 7 edges: 40%; note equivalence after swapping parts: 10%.

q_graph_bipartite_03.title: Bipartite graphs need not be connected or have even edge counts
q_graph_bipartite_03.statement: Which statements about finite undirected simple graphs are correct?
q_graph_bipartite_03.explanation: A is true: trees have no cycles and hence no odd cycles. B is false: two disjoint edges form a disconnected bipartite graph. C is false: K₂ has just 1 edge and is bipartite. D is true: every step changes parts, so an odd number of steps ends in the other part and cannot return to the start.
q_graph_bipartite_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for exactly A,D. When explanations are required, each of the four judgments may be scored separately.

options.text: Every tree is bipartite.
Every bipartite graph is connected.
Every bipartite graph has an even number of edges.
A bipartite graph has no odd-length closed walk.

q_graph_bipartite_04.title: Proving the no-odd-cycle criterion
q_graph_bipartite_04.statement: Prove that a finite undirected simple graph G is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle. G may be disconnected.
q_graph_bipartite_04.answer_text: If G has a bipartition, every edge along a cycle switches parts. Returning to the start requires an even number of edges, so no odd cycle exists. Conversely, suppose G has no odd cycle. Choose a root and a search tree in every component and color vertices by parity of tree distance from the root. If an original edge uv had equal-colored endpoints, the unique tree path from u to v would have even length. The edge is not a tree edge; adding it to the path yields an odd cycle, a contradiction. Thus every original edge joins different colors. Combining equal color classes across all components gives a bipartition of G.
q_graph_bipartite_04.explanation: The forward direction uses a change of part at every edge. The reverse must handle every component and combine an equal-color edge with a tree path to get an actual simple odd cycle.
q_graph_bipartite_04.grading_criteria: Forward proof: 25%; componentwise coloring construction: 30%; obtain an odd cycle from an equal-color edge: 30%; combine components and conclude: 15%.

q_graph_bipartite_05.title: Vertices, edges, and degrees in a complete bipartite graph
q_graph_bipartite_05.statement: Find the vertex count, edge count, and degrees in both parts of K₃,₅. If any 3 edges are deleted, must the remaining graph still be bipartite?
q_graph_bipartite_05.answer_text: There are 3+5=8 vertices and 3·5=15 edges. Each vertex in the size-3 part has degree 5; each in the size-5 part has degree 3. Deleting any 3 edges preserves bipartiteness, since the original partition still makes every remaining edge cross parts.
q_graph_bipartite_05.explanation: Bipartiteness restricts edge locations without requiring all possible cross-part edges. Edge deletion preserves this property.
q_graph_bipartite_05.grading_criteria: Vertex and edge counts: 40%; degrees in both parts: 30%; deletion conclusion and justification: 30%.

q_graph_bipartite_06.title: Even degrees do not ensure bipartiteness
q_graph_bipartite_06.statement: Is the statement “A finite undirected simple graph with all degrees even is bipartite” true? If false, give an explicit counterexample on at least 5 vertices and justify it.
q_graph_bipartite_06.answer_text: It is false. Take C₅ with edges 12,23,34,45,51. Every vertex has even degree 2, but the whole graph is a 5-edge odd cycle, violating the no-odd-cycle criterion for bipartite graphs.
q_graph_bipartite_06.explanation: Degree parity is local edge-count information; bipartiteness restricts parity of cycle lengths. One cannot replace the other.
q_graph_bipartite_06.grading_criteria: Declare false: 20%; counterexample satisfying at least 5 vertices: 40%; check both even degrees and nonbipartiteness: 40%.

q_graph_bipartite_07.title: A bipartiteness test must search every component
q_graph_bipartite_07.statement: A graph has vertices {a,b,c,x,y,z,t} and edges {ab,bc,xy,yz,zx}. A program performs one two-coloring search from a and declares the whole graph bipartite. Identify the omission and show a conflicting edge or odd cycle.
q_graph_bipartite_07.answer_text: The program checks only {a,b,c}, missing the triangle component {x,y,z} and isolated t. Starting x with color 0 forces y,z both to color 1, so yz is a conflicting equal-color edge. Equivalently, x−y−z−x is an odd cycle. Thus the graph is not bipartite. Vertex t may have either color and does not cause the failure.
q_graph_bipartite_07.explanation: For disconnected graphs, visit every unvisited vertex. Two-colorability of one component does not imply that of the whole graph.
q_graph_bipartite_07.grading_criteria: Identify unvisited components: 30%; exhibit the triangle or equal-color conflict: 50%; explain arbitrary coloring of the isolated vertex: 20%.

q_graph_bipartite_08.title: Directly constructing a bipartition of a forest
q_graph_bipartite_08.statement: Without citing “bipartite if and only if no odd cycle,” prove that every finite undirected simple forest is bipartite. Isolated vertices are allowed.
q_graph_bipartite_08.answer_text: Choose a root in each tree component. Put vertices at even root distance in L and those at odd distance in R. Each tree edge joins a vertex to its parent, whose root distance differs by 1, so its endpoints lie in different parts. An isolated vertex has distance 0 from its own root and may go in L. Apply the rule to all components: L,R are disjoint, cover all vertices, and every edge crosses parts. Thus the forest is bipartite.
q_graph_bipartite_08.explanation: The parent-edge structure comes from unique paths toward the root. Directly proving every edge crosses parity layers verifies the bipartition.
q_graph_bipartite_08.grading_criteria: Choose roots componentwise and partition by parity: 35%; prove edges join consecutive levels: 40%; handle isolated vertices and combine all components: 25%.

q_graph_topological_01.title: Which vertices may come next in topological sorting?
q_graph_topological_01.statement: In Kahn’s topological sorting of a finite DAG, which kind of vertex can be output next? Degrees refer to the current graph after previous deletions.
q_graph_topological_01.explanation: Indegree 0 means there is no unprocessed prerequisite, so the vertex can come next. Delete its outgoing arcs and update successor indegrees. Outdegree 0 means no successors, not that prerequisites are satisfied.

options.text: A vertex of outdegree 0.
A vertex of indegree 0.
A vertex of maximum indegree.
Any vertex not yet output.

q_graph_topological_02.title: Enumerating topological orders with merging dependencies
q_graph_topological_02.statement: A directed graph has vertices {a,b,c,d,e} and arcs {a→c,b→c,b→d,c→e,d→e}. List every topological order, treating distinct labeled sequences as different.
q_graph_topological_02.answer_text: There are 5: a,b,c,d,e; a,b,d,c,e; b,a,c,d,e; b,a,d,c,e; b,d,a,c,e. Vertex e must follow c,d and is therefore last. If a is first, b must be second and c,d may be swapped, giving 2 orders. If b is first, the second vertex is a or d, yielding 2 and 1 orders respectively, hence 3. Total: 5.
q_graph_topological_02.explanation: Branch over current zero-indegree candidates to produce the sequences and prove completeness. Only a,b can initially come first.
q_graph_topological_02.grading_criteria: Each distinct correct order: 12%, totaling 60%; complete branching count and justification of no omissions: 40%.

q_graph_topological_03.title: Properties of topological orders and cycle detection
q_graph_topological_03.statement: Which statements about finite directed graphs are correct?
q_graph_topological_03.explanation: A is true by transitivity of the order along a path. B is false: a→b,a→c has only initial candidate a, but b,c can be swapped. C is true because all arcs remain forward in that order and cannot form a cycle. D is true: any finite acyclic remainder has a zero-indegree vertex, so stopping early means a cycle remains.
q_graph_topological_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for exactly A,C,D. Selecting B precludes full credit.

options.text: A topological order puts the start of every directed path before its end.
If there is just one initial zero-indegree vertex, the topological order must be unique.
Adding to a DAG an arc from an earlier to a later vertex in one topological order preserves directed acyclicity.
If Kahn’s algorithm outputs fewer vertices than the total, the original graph has a directed cycle.

q_graph_topological_04.title: Proving every DAG has a topological order
q_graph_topological_04.statement: Prove that every finite DAG has a topological order. Explain why each nonempty remaining graph must have a zero-indegree vertex.
q_graph_topological_04.answer_text: First, any nonempty finite DAG has a zero-indegree vertex. Otherwise, start anywhere and repeatedly follow an incoming arc to a predecessor. Finiteness forces a repeated vertex; the repeated section, in original arc direction, gives a directed cycle, a contradiction. Now induct on vertex count. The empty graph has the empty order. In a nonempty DAG, delete a zero-indegree vertex v and its outgoing arcs. The remainder is still a DAG and has a topological order by induction. Put v first. No arc enters v, all arcs out of v go forward, and all remaining arcs go forward in the inductive order, giving a topological order of the original graph.
q_graph_topological_04.explanation: Predecessors must be found along incoming arcs. Finiteness forces repetition, and deletion cannot create a cycle.
q_graph_topological_04.grading_criteria: Contradiction establishing a zero-indegree vertex: 40%; empty base and deletion induction: 30%; verify all arcs in the combined order: 30%.

q_graph_topological_05.title: Does adding a dependency create a cycle?
q_graph_topological_05.statement: A DAG has arcs {a→b,a→c,b→d,c→d,d→e}. Starting independently from the original graph, (1) add b→c; (2) add e→a. Decide whether each result remains a DAG, with reasons. The additions are independent.
q_graph_topological_05.answer_text: (1) It remains a DAG: a,b,c,d,e is a topological order, with all arcs forward. (2) It is no longer a DAG, since a→b→d→e→a is a directed cycle. In general, adding u→v creates a cycle if and only if the original graph has a directed path from v to u.
q_graph_topological_05.explanation: Check each addition separately; do not include the first new edge when answering the second part. A complete topological order proves acyclicity, and an explicit directed cycle disproves it.
q_graph_topological_05.grading_criteria: First conclusion and topological order: 45%; second conclusion and cycle: 45%; acknowledge independent operations: 10%.

q_graph_topological_06.title: Lexicographic zero-indegree deletion
q_graph_topological_06.statement: A directed graph has arcs {a→c,b→c,c→d,c→e,d→f,e→f}. At every step select the alphabetically smallest current zero-indegree candidate. Give Kahn’s output and initial indegrees.
q_graph_topological_06.answer_text: Initial indegrees: a:0,b:0,c:2,d:1,e:1,f:2. Output a then b, reducing c to indegree 0. After c, both d,e are candidates; choose d then e. Only after deleting e→f does f reach indegree 0. The final order is a,b,c,d,e,f.
q_graph_topological_06.explanation: Alphabetic order only breaks ties between valid candidates. It cannot justify outputting a positive-indegree vertex early.
q_graph_topological_06.grading_criteria: Six initial indegrees: 40%; valid output order: 35%; explain when c,f enter the candidate set: 25%.

q_graph_topological_07.title: Testing uniqueness with consecutive arcs
q_graph_topological_07.statement: Let v₁,…,vₙ be a topological order of a finite DAG. Prove that it is the unique topological order if and only if vᵢ→vᵢ₊₁ is an arc for every i<n.
q_graph_topological_07.answer_text: If every consecutive arc exists, they form a directed chain through all vertices. Every topological order must put v₁ before v₂, v₂ before v₃, and so on, forcing this unique order. Conversely, suppose the order is unique but some consecutive pair lacks vᵢ→vᵢ₊₁. The reverse arc is also absent, or the given order would be invalid. Swap these consecutive entries. Only their relative order changes; neither crosses any other vertex. Since there is no arc between them, all arc constraints remain satisfied, giving a different topological order, a contradiction. Thus all consecutive arcs exist.
q_graph_topological_07.explanation: Swapping consecutive entries does not cross a third vertex, which is key to the reverse argument. For n≤1, both conditions hold naturally.
q_graph_topological_07.grading_criteria: Directed chain forces uniqueness: 35%; rule out a reverse arc: 15%; prove the adjacent swap valid and derive contradiction: 40%; boundary cases: 10%.

q_graph_topological_08.title: Counting schedules of two independent task chains
q_graph_topological_08.statement: Four distinct tasks a,b,c,d have only constraints a→b,c→d and no other arcs. Count topological orders and list them all.
q_graph_topological_08.answer_text: There are 6: a,b,c,d; a,c,b,d; a,c,d,b; c,a,b,d; c,a,d,b; c,d,a,b. Choose 2 of the 4 positions for a,b in that order, then put c,d in order in the rest. Thus the count is C(4,2)=6.
q_graph_topological_08.explanation: The internal order in each chain is fixed, but the chains may interleave. Neither all 4! permutations nor treating the chains as two indivisible blocks gives the correct count.
q_graph_topological_08.grading_criteria: Correct count 6: 30%; six distinct orders: 40%; exhaustive interleaving argument: 30%.

q_graph_domination_01.title: Isolated vertices and three types of vertex sets
q_graph_domination_01.statement: Which statement about dominating sets, vertex covers, and independent sets in finite undirected simple graphs is always true?
q_graph_domination_01.explanation: An isolated vertex outside a dominating set cannot neighbor any vertex inside, so it must belong to every dominating set. Independent sets need not dominate the graph; vertex covers may have internal edges. A triangle has domination number 1 and vertex-cover number 2, so these minima generally differ.

options.text: Every independent set is dominating.
Every isolated vertex belongs to every dominating set.
Every vertex cover is independent.
The minimum dominating-set size always equals the minimum vertex-cover size.

q_graph_domination_02.title: Domination, vertex cover, and independence on a path
q_graph_domination_02.statement: The undirected simple path P₆ has vertices 1,…,6 and edges 12,23,34,45,56. Find γ(P₆),τ(P₆),α(P₆), giving a set attaining each. Cover means vertex cover.
q_graph_domination_02.answer_text: γ(P₆)=2, attained by D={2,5}, covering {1,2,3} and {4,5,6}. One vertex covers at most 3 vertices and cannot dominate all 6. Also τ(P₆)=3, attained by C={2,4,6}. The disjoint edges 12,34,56 require at least 3 covering vertices. Finally α(P₆)=3, attained by I={1,3,5}. Each pair {1,2},{3,4},{5,6} contributes at most one independent vertex, so more than 3 is impossible.
q_graph_domination_02.explanation: For each optimum, give a feasible construction and a bound ruling out a better one. Listing one set alone does not establish optimality.
q_graph_domination_02.grading_criteria: Each of the three values: 15%, totaling 45%; each witness set: 10%, totaling 30%; corresponding optimality arguments: 25%.

q_graph_domination_03.title: Complements of independent sets and vertex covers
q_graph_domination_03.statement: Let G=(V,E) be a finite undirected simple graph. Prove C⊆V is a vertex cover if and only if V∖C is independent, then deduce τ(G)+α(G)=|V|.
q_graph_domination_03.answer_text: If C covers every edge, no edge has both endpoints in V∖C, so V∖C is independent. Conversely, if V∖C is independent, every edge has at least one endpoint in C, making C a vertex cover. Let n=|V|. The complement of a minimum cover is independent, giving n−τ≤α. The complement of a maximum independent set is a cover, giving τ≤n−α, or α≤n−τ. Together α=n−τ, hence τ+α=n.
q_graph_domination_03.explanation: First prove the complement correspondence for individual sets. Then turn minimization and maximization into inequalities in both directions to justify equality of optimal values.
q_graph_domination_03.grading_criteria: Each direction of the set equivalence: 25%; each optimal-value inequality: 20%; final equality: 10%.

q_graph_domination_04.title: Why a maximal independent set need not be maximum
q_graph_domination_04.statement: In K₁,₄, let c be the center and u₁,u₂,u₃,u₄ the leaves. (1) Explain why {c} is maximal independent but not maximum. (2) Prove every maximal independent set in any finite undirected simple graph is dominating.
q_graph_domination_04.answer_text: (1) The set {c} is independent, but every leaf neighbors c and cannot be added, so it is maximal. All four leaves form an independent set of size 4, so {c} is not maximum. (2) Let I be maximal independent. If some v∈V∖I had no neighbor in I, then I∪{v} would remain independent, contradicting maximality. Thus every outside vertex has a neighbor in I, so I dominates.
q_graph_domination_04.explanation: Maximal means it cannot be enlarged by adding elements, not that it is largest among all independent sets. The second part uses this inclusion maximality.
q_graph_domination_04.grading_criteria: Maximality of the singleton center: 25%; a larger independent set: 20%; general contradiction proof and domination conclusion: 55%.

q_graph_domination_05.title: A minimum dominating set of a 7-cycle
q_graph_domination_05.statement: The undirected simple cycle C₇ has edges 12,23,34,45,56,67,71. Find its domination number, a minimum dominating set, and a proof of optimality.
q_graph_domination_05.answer_text: γ(C₇)=3. Each vertex and its neighbors consist of exactly 3 vertices, so two selected vertices cover at most 6 and at least 3 selections are needed. For D={1,4,6}, the closed neighborhoods are {7,1,2},{3,4,5},{5,6,7}; their union is all 7 vertices, so 3 suffice.
q_graph_domination_05.explanation: The lower bound uses “at most 6,” allowing overlap of closed neighborhoods. Verify the construction covers every vertex to obtain a matching upper bound.
q_graph_domination_05.grading_criteria: Lower bound 3: 40%; feasible 3-vertex set with explicit checking: 40%; domination number: 20%.

q_graph_domination_06.title: Covering after adding an isolated vertex
q_graph_domination_06.statement: G consists of triangle a−b−c−a and isolated z. Find its minimum vertex-cover size and decide whether z must belong to a minimum cover. Compare with the requirement on z for minimum dominating sets.
q_graph_domination_06.answer_text: The minimum vertex-cover size is 2, for example {a,b}. One triangle vertex misses the edge between the other two, so at least 2 are needed. Since z has no incident edge, it need not belong to a minimum cover. A dominating set must include z, or z outside it would have no neighbor. Adding any one triangle vertex suffices, so the minimum dominating-set size is also 2, but that set must include z.
q_graph_domination_06.explanation: The two minima happen to agree here, while their conditions and constructions differ: vertex covers concern edges and domination concerns vertices.
q_graph_domination_06.grading_criteria: Cover number and lower bound: 35%; explain why z is unnecessary for a cover: 25%; domination’s requirement on z and a construction: 40%.

q_graph_domination_07.title: Subsets and complements of independent sets
q_graph_domination_07.statement: Which assertions about independent sets in finite undirected simple graphs always hold?
q_graph_domination_07.explanation: A fails: in a single edge ab, {a},{b} are independent but their union is not. B holds because taking a subset introduces no internal edges. C holds because otherwise some edge would lie entirely within the independent set. D fails: in K₁,₄ both the singleton center and the larger set of four leaves are maximal independent sets.
q_graph_domination_07.grading_criteria: Full credit for exactly B,C. Counterexamples must verify both the premises and the failure of the conclusion.

options.text: The union of two independent sets is independent.
Every subset of an independent set is independent.
The complement of an independent set is a vertex cover.
All maximal independent sets have the same number of vertices.

q_graph_domination_08.title: A 4-cycle with an isolated vertex
q_graph_domination_08.statement: G consists of cycle a−b−c−d−a and isolated z. Find α(G),τ(G),γ(G), giving an optimal set and a proof that no better one exists for each.
q_graph_domination_08.answer_text: α(G)=3, attained by {a,c,z}. Each adjacent pair {a,b},{c,d} contributes at most one vertex, plus z, so at most 3 are possible. Also τ(G)=2, attained by {a,c}; disjoint edges ab,cd require at least 2 covering vertices. Finally γ(G)=3, attained by {a,c,z}. Vertex z is mandatory, and one cycle vertex covers only itself and its two neighbors, not all 4 cycle vertices, so at least 2 additional vertices are needed.
q_graph_domination_08.explanation: The isolated vertex increases independence and domination numbers by 1 but does not increase the vertex-cover number. Check the first two values using α+τ=5.
q_graph_domination_08.grading_criteria: Each value: 15%, totaling 45%; three feasible sets: 30%; three lower-bound arguments and the isolated vertex’s role: 25%.

q_graph_matching_01.title: What type of matching is the middle edge?
q_graph_matching_01.statement: In the path 1−2−3−4, take M={23}. Which judgment is correct?
q_graph_matching_01.explanation: Both 12 and 34 share an endpoint with 23 and cannot be added directly, so M is maximal. But {12,34} has 2 edges and is larger, so M is not maximum and is not perfect.

options.text: M is both maximum and perfect.
M is maximal but not maximum.
M is not maximal.
M covers all 4 vertices.

q_graph_matching_02.title: Enlarging a matching along an augmenting path
q_graph_matching_02.statement: A bipartite graph has left part {a,b,c,d}, right part {1,2,3,4}, and N(a)={1,2},N(b)={2},N(c)={2,3},N(d)={3,4}. Given M={a2,c3,d4}, find an augmenting path, the augmented matching, and decide whether it is maximum.
q_graph_matching_02.answer_text: The path b−2−a−1 is augmenting: b,1 are unmatched, b2,a1 are outside M, and 2a is in M. Remove a2 and add b2,a1, giving M′={a1,b2,c3,d4}. It has 4 edges and covers both parts completely, so it is perfect. No matching has more than 4 edges, so it is also maximum.
q_graph_matching_02.explanation: Flip membership along the path; do not keep a2 while adding a1,b2.
q_graph_matching_02.grading_criteria: Valid augmenting path and alternation: 40%; new matching: 35%; explain perfection and maximum size: 25%.

q_graph_matching_03.title: Hall obstructions from shared neighbors
q_graph_matching_03.statement: A bipartite graph has L={a,b,c},R={1,2,3}, with N(a)=N(b)={1},N(c)={2,3}. Which statements are correct?
q_graph_matching_03.explanation: A is false: individual neighbors do not ensure distinct partners for several vertices. B is true: {a,b} has only neighbor 1. C is true: at most one of a,b can be matched, plus c, for at most 2 edges; {a1,c2} attains 2. D is true: after adding b2, take {a1,b2,c3}.
q_graph_matching_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for exactly B,C,D. Matching witnesses and the shortage of neighbors may be credited as reasoning.

options.text: Every left vertex has a neighbor, so a matching saturating L must exist.
S={a,b} violates Hall’s condition.
The original graph has maximum matching size 2.
After adding b2, a perfect matching exists.

q_graph_matching_04.title: The maximum-matching augmenting-path criterion
q_graph_matching_04.statement: Prove that a matching M in a finite undirected simple graph is maximum if and only if there is no M-augmenting path.
q_graph_matching_04.answer_text: If an augmenting path exists, flipping its matching and nonmatching edges gives a matching with one more edge, so M is not maximum. Conversely, if M is not maximum, choose a larger matching M′. In the symmetric-difference subgraph M△M′, every vertex has degree at most 2, and each nontrivial component is an alternating path or even cycle. Cycles have equal numbers of the two edge types. Since |M′|>|M|, some path has one more M′ edge than M edge. Its first and last edges are in M′, and both endpoints are unmatched by M: any incident M edge not common to both matchings would extend this component, while a common edge would conflict with the endpoint’s M′ edge. Thus this path is M-augmenting, a contradiction. Hence no augmenting path implies M is maximum.
q_graph_matching_04.explanation: Alternating symmetric-difference components locate the total edge-count difference on a path. Prove its endpoints unmatched; saying merely “alternating” is insufficient.
q_graph_matching_04.grading_criteria: Flipping direction: 25%; symmetric-difference component structure: 30%; derive a suitable path from the count difference: 20%; prove unmatched endpoints and conclude: 25%.

q_graph_matching_05.title: Even order and no isolated vertices do not ensure perfection
q_graph_matching_05.statement: Which 4-vertex undirected simple graph has no isolated vertices but no perfect matching?
q_graph_matching_05.explanation: Every edge of K₁,₃ shares the center, so a matching has at most 1 edge and cannot cover 4 vertices. Each of C₄,P₄,K₂,₂ has two disjoint edges covering all vertices.

options.text: The star K₁,₃.
The cycle C₄.
The path P₄.
The complete bipartite graph K₂,₂.

q_graph_matching_06.title: A five-edge augmenting path
q_graph_matching_06.statement: A bipartite graph has L={a,b,c},R={1,2,3}, edge set {a1,a2,b2,b3,c1}, and matching M={a1,b2}. Give an augmenting path and the flipped matching.
q_graph_matching_06.answer_text: An augmenting path is c−1−a−2−b−3. Its endpoints c,3 are unmatched, and its edges alternate nonmatching,matching,nonmatching,matching,nonmatching. Remove a1,b2 and add c1,a2,b3. The result {c1,a2,b3} is perfect, with size increasing from 2 to 3.
q_graph_matching_06.explanation: No edge can simply be added; the partners of two matched vertices must be reassigned.
q_graph_matching_06.grading_criteria: Complete valid path: 40%; correctly remove old edges and add new ones: 40%; check size increase and perfection: 20%.

q_graph_matching_07.title: How many edges repair a Hall deficiency?
q_graph_matching_07.statement: A bipartite graph has L={a,b,c,d},R={1,2,3,4}, with N(a)=N(b)=N(c)={1},N(d)={2,3,4}. Previously absent cross-part edges may be added. What is the minimum number needed for a perfect matching? Give a construction attaining the bound.
q_graph_matching_07.answer_text: At least 2 are needed. For S={a,b,c}, initially |N(S)|=1, while Hall requires at least 3 distinct neighbors. Each new edge adds at most one vertex to N(S), so fewer than 2 cannot fix this obstruction. Add b2,c3; then {a1,b2,c3,d4} is perfect, so 2 suffice.
q_graph_matching_07.explanation: Fixing one necessary obstruction does not automatically ensure success. Supply a matching covering every vertex to establish feasibility of the construction.
q_graph_matching_07.grading_criteria: Identify the deficient subset: 25%; prove at least 2 edges: 35%; two new edges and a perfect matching: 40%.

q_graph_matching_08.title: Matchings give a lower bound on vertex covers
q_graph_matching_08.statement: Prove ν(G)≤τ(G) for every finite undirected simple graph. Give one concrete graph with equality and one with strict inequality, computing both values.
q_graph_matching_08.answer_text: Let M be any matching and C any vertex cover. Each edge of M needs an endpoint in C. Matching edges share no endpoint, so these selected endpoints are distinct and |M|≤|C|. Taking a maximum matching and minimum cover gives ν≤τ. For equality take K₂,₃: maximum matching size is 2, and the size-2 part covers every edge, so ν=τ=2. For strict inequality take K₃: every two edges share an endpoint, so ν=1, but covering all three edges needs at least 2 vertices, so τ=2 and 1<2.
q_graph_matching_08.explanation: The inequality holds for general graphs; equality for bipartite graphs must not be extended to all graphs.
q_graph_matching_08.grading_criteria: General inequality proof: 50%; equality example with both values: 25%; strict example with both values: 25%.

q_tree_basic_01.title: Edges in a forest
q_tree_basic_01.statement: A finite undirected simple forest has 14 vertices and 4 connected components, counting isolated vertices as components. It has ____ edges.
q_tree_basic_01.explanation: Each component is a tree. Summing “vertices minus 1” over components gives m=n−c=14−4=10.
q_tree_basic_01.grading_criteria: Full credit for 10. For reasoning, split credit equally between the formula and component explanation.

q_tree_basic_02.title: Tree tests that retain the required conditions
q_tree_basic_02.statement: Each option describes a finite undirected simple graph with 6 vertices. Which guarantees a tree?
q_tree_basic_02.explanation: Acyclicity with n−1=5 edges is equivalent to being a tree. A is connected with 6 edges and must contain a cycle; B is disconnected; D has 7 edges, exceeding a tree’s 5.

options.text: Connected with 6 edges.
Disconnected with 5 edges.
Acyclic with 5 edges.
Connected with 7 edges.

q_tree_basic_03.title: Counting leaves from branching vertices
q_tree_basic_03.statement: An undirected simple tree has 12 vertices, exactly 3 of degree 3, and all others of degree 1 or 2. Find the numbers of degree-1 and degree-2 vertices.
q_tree_basic_03.answer_text: Let the counts be x,y. Vertex counting gives x+y+3=12 and the handshake lemma gives x+2y+3·3=2·11=22. Thus x+y=9 and x+2y=13; subtraction gives y=4 and then x=5. There are 5 leaves and 4 degree-2 vertices.
q_tree_basic_03.explanation: A tree is connected and has more than one vertex, so it has no degree-0 vertex. Two independent counting equations determine the unknowns.
q_tree_basic_03.grading_criteria: Vertex-count equation: 25%; degree-sum equation: 35%; solve x=5,y=4 and interpret: 40%.

q_tree_basic_04.title: Endpoints of a longest path are leaves
q_tree_basic_04.statement: Prove every finite undirected simple tree with at least 2 vertices has at least two degree-1 vertices.
q_tree_basic_04.answer_text: Choose a simple path P of maximum edge count. It has at least one edge and distinct endpoints u,v. If u had a neighbor w besides its next vertex on P, then w cannot be another vertex of P, since the edge and part of P would make a cycle. Nor can w lie outside P, since prepending w would produce a longer simple path. Thus u has just its one neighbor on P and degree 1. The same holds for v. Since u≠v, the tree has at least two leaves.
q_tree_basic_04.explanation: Exclude extra neighbors both on and off the path, using acyclicity and maximal length respectively.
q_tree_basic_04.grading_criteria: Choose a longest path with distinct endpoints: 20%; exclude both neighbor cases: 50%; apply the same argument at the other end and conclude: 30%.

q_tree_basic_05.title: The count n−1 alone is insufficient
q_tree_basic_05.statement: Construct a finite undirected simple graph with exactly 6 vertices and 5 edges that is not a tree. Give its vertex and edge sets and identify the tree-definition conditions it violates.
q_tree_basic_05.answer_text: Take V={a,b,c,d,e,f}, E={ab,bc,ca,de,ef}. It has 6 vertices and 5 edges. Vertices {a,b,c} form a triangle and {d,e,f} a path, with no edge between them. It is both cyclic and disconnected, so it is not a tree.
q_tree_basic_05.explanation: The condition m=n−1 must be combined with connectivity or acyclicity. This counterexample shows how failures of the two conditions can offset one another in the edge count.
q_tree_basic_05.grading_criteria: Required vertex and edge counts: 40%; simplicity: 10%; correctly explain both disconnection and a cycle: 50%.

q_tree_basic_06.title: Deleting and joining forest components
q_tree_basic_06.statement: A forest F has 18 vertices and 11 edges. Delete two distinct edges, then add 3 new edges in sequence, each joining different components at that moment. Find the initial component count, the count after deletions, the final count, and the final edge count.
q_tree_basic_06.answer_text: Initially c=18−11=7. Every forest edge is a bridge of its tree component, so deleting two leaves 9 components and 9 edges. Each addition joins different components, reducing their number by 1 without creating a cycle. Finally c=6 and m=12; check 18−6=12.
q_tree_basic_06.explanation: No operation changes the vertex count. Requiring endpoints in different current components ensures every step still gives a forest.
q_tree_basic_06.grading_criteria: Initial component count: 25%; count after deletion: 30%; final components and edges with a check: 45%.

q_tree_basic_07.title: Leaves with several branching degrees
q_tree_basic_07.statement: A finite undirected simple tree on 15 vertices has exactly two degree-4 vertices and one degree-3 vertex. Every other degree is 1 or 2. Find the numbers of leaves and degree-2 vertices.
q_tree_basic_07.answer_text: Let x count leaves and y count degree-2 vertices. Then x+y+2+1=15, so x+y=12. The degree sum is 2·14=28, giving x+2y+8+3=28, or x+2y=17. Subtract to obtain y=5, hence x=7.
q_tree_basic_07.explanation: Alternatively, use n₁=2+Σₖ≥₃(k−2)nₖ to get n₁=2+2·2+1=7 directly, then find the remaining count.
q_tree_basic_07.grading_criteria: Correct vertex and degree constraints: 55%; 7 leaves and 5 degree-2 vertices: 35%; verification or equivalent formula: 10%.

q_tree_basic_08.title: Why connectedness and n−1 edges imply a tree
q_tree_basic_08.statement: Prove that a finite connected undirected simple graph on n≥1 vertices with exactly n−1 edges is a tree. Explain why a cycle is impossible instead of merely repeating the equivalent characterization.
q_tree_basic_08.answer_text: First, any connected n-vertex graph has at least n−1 edges. Start from one vertex and enlarge the reached set, recording an edge from the old set whenever a new vertex is reached. Connectivity permits this until n−1 distinct edges have been recorded. If the given graph had a cycle, delete one cycle edge. The rest of the cycle still connects its endpoints, so the whole graph remains connected but has only n−2 edges, contradicting the bound. Thus it is acyclic and connected, hence a tree by definition. For n=1 there are no edges, and it is likewise connected and acyclic.
q_tree_basic_08.explanation: The key is the conflict between the minimum edge count for connectivity and preserving connectivity on deleting a cycle edge, not simply citing the characterization to be proved.
q_tree_basic_08.grading_criteria: Prove the connected-graph edge lower bound: 40%; delete a cycle edge and derive an edge-count contradiction: 40%; conclusion and n=1 case: 20%.

q_tree_rooted_01.title: Rooted-tree height and leaves
q_tree_rooted_01.statement: A tree has root r with children a,b; a has children c,d; b has only child e; there are no other vertices. Measuring depth and height in edges, its height is ____ and its leaf set is ____.
q_tree_rooted_01.explanation: Root depth is 0; a,b have depth 1 and c,d,e depth 2, the maximum. Leaves have no children; b still has a child and is not a leaf.
q_tree_rooted_01.grading_criteria: Height 2: 40%; complete leaf set: 60%. Including b precludes full credit.

q_tree_rooted_02.title: Counting a full ternary tree
q_tree_rooted_02.statement: A finite full ternary tree has exactly 3 children at each internal vertex and 7 internal vertices. Find total vertices and leaves. The leaves need not have equal depth.
q_tree_rooted_02.answer_text: Every nonroot vertex has exactly one parent, so there are n−1 edges. The 7 internal vertices each contribute 3 parent–child edges, giving 21 edges. Thus n=22 and l=n−7=15 leaves.
q_tree_rooted_02.explanation: Only the requirement of exactly 3 children per internal vertex is used, without balance or equal leaf depths.
q_tree_rooted_02.grading_criteria: Two ways of counting edges: 50%; total vertices 22 and leaves 15: 25% each.

q_tree_rooted_03.title: Rerooting changes height and rooted-tree leaves
q_tree_rooted_03.statement: For the undirected simple path A−B−C−D−E, find the height and leaf set when rooted at A and at C. Do the degree-1 vertices of the underlying graph change? Measure height in edges; a rooted-tree leaf has no children.
q_tree_rooted_03.answer_text: Rooted at A, height is 4 and the sole rooted-tree leaf is E. Although A has undirected degree 1, it has child B. Rooted at C, height is 2 and leaves are A,E. The underlying graph is unchanged, so its degree-1 vertices remain A,E.
q_tree_rooted_03.explanation: Changing the root changes parent directions and depths but not undirected edges or degrees. Distinguish rooted-tree leaves from degree-1 vertices of an undirected tree.
q_tree_rooted_03.grading_criteria: Height and leaves for each root: 35%; distinguish undirected degree from the root’s children: 30%.

q_tree_rooted_04.title: Deriving the full binary-tree formula by counting children
q_tree_rooted_04.statement: Prove that in any nonempty finite rooted tree, the sum of all child counts is n−1. Deduce that if every internal vertex has exactly 2 children, the leaf count l equals the internal count i plus 1. A one-vertex tree is allowed.
q_tree_rooted_04.answer_text: Every vertex except the root has one parent, and each parent–child edge is counted once at its parent. Thus total child count equals the number of nonroot vertices n−1. In a full binary tree, each internal vertex contributes 2 and each leaf 0, so 2i=n−1. Since n=i+l, this gives 2i=i+l−1 and l=i+1. A single-root tree has i=0,l=1 and also satisfies the formula.
q_tree_rooted_04.explanation: Child count is not undirected degree sum: degrees count each edge twice, while children count it just once at the parent.
q_tree_rooted_04.grading_criteria: One-to-one counting argument: 50%; equations 2i=n−1 and n=i+l: 25%; derive the formula and handle a single root: 25%.

q_tree_rooted_05.title: Parents, ancestors, and subtrees
q_tree_rooted_05.statement: A rooted tree has r’s children a,b; a’s children c,d; b’s child e; and c’s child f, with no other edges. Find f’s parent and all ancestors, the vertices of a’s subtree, and the lowest common ancestor of d,f. Ancestors exclude the vertex itself.
q_tree_rooted_05.answer_text: The parent of f is c. The parent chain f→c→a→r gives ancestors {c,a,r}. The subtree at a has vertices {a,c,d,f}. The common ancestors of d,f are a,r; the nearer is a, so their lowest common ancestor is a.
q_tree_rooted_05.explanation: A parent is just one level up; ancestors comprise the whole upward chain. A subtree extends downward and includes its root and all descendants.
q_tree_rooted_05.grading_criteria: The four parts: 20%,30%,30%,20% respectively. Deduct the corresponding credit if f is incorrectly included among its ancestors.

q_tree_rooted_06.title: Computing depth separately from subtree height
q_tree_rooted_06.statement: A tree rooted at r has edges {ra,rb,ac,cd,be,ef}. In edge units, find depths of d,f, height of the whole tree, depth of a, and height of a’s subtree.
q_tree_rooted_06.answer_text: The root paths are r−a−c−d and r−b−e−f. Both d,f have depth 3, and the tree has height 3. Vertex a has depth 1. Its subtree is a−c−d and has height 2.
q_tree_rooted_06.explanation: Depth of a starts from the whole-tree root r; height of a’s subtree starts at a and takes the maximum downward distance. The starting point and direction differ.
q_tree_rooted_06.grading_criteria: Depths of d,f together: 30%; whole-tree height: 20%; a’s depth: 20%; a-subtree height and the distinction: 30%.

q_tree_rooted_07.title: A divisibility condition for full 4-ary trees
q_tree_rooted_07.statement: In a full 4-ary tree, every internal vertex has exactly 4 children. (1) With 22 leaves, find internal and total vertex counts. (2) Can such a tree have 23 leaves? Explain.
q_tree_rooted_07.answer_text: A full 4-ary tree satisfies l=3i+1. If l=22, then i=(22−1)/3=7 and n=i+l=29. If l=23, then i=22/3 is not an integer, so no such full 4-ary tree exists.
q_tree_rooted_07.explanation: The leaf count must be congruent to 1 modulo 3. This necessary divisibility condition comes from parent–child edge counting, not balance.
q_tree_rooted_07.grading_criteria: Formula and both values in part 1: 60%; integrality contradiction in part 2: 40%.

q_tree_rooted_08.title: Depth sums and ancestor–descendant pairs
q_tree_rooted_08.statement: Let T be a nonempty finite rooted tree, with root depth 0 and no vertex its own ancestor. Prove that the sum of vertex depths equals the number of ordered pairs (u,v) with u an ancestor of v. Check this for r−a−b rooted at r.
q_tree_rooted_08.answer_text: Fix v. Its root path has depth(v) edges and exactly depth(v) vertices other than v. These are precisely its ancestors, so there are depth(v) valid ordered pairs with second entry v. Summing over v counts each pair once by its second entry, giving Σᵥdepth(v). In the example the depths 0,1,2 sum to 3; the pairs (r,a),(r,b),(a,b) also number 3.
q_tree_rooted_08.explanation: Exclude each vertex as its own ancestor; otherwise each would add a self-pair and the count would be larger by n.
q_tree_rooted_08.grading_criteria: Count for a fixed second entry: 45%; explain no repetition or omission and sum: 30%; example and ancestor convention: 25%.

q_tree_spanning_01.title: Which edge set is a spanning tree?
q_tree_spanning_01.statement: An undirected simple graph G has vertices {a,b,c,d} and edges {ab,bc,ca,cd}. Which edge set, together with all 4 original vertices, forms a spanning tree?
q_tree_spanning_01.explanation: A gives the connected acyclic path a−b−c−d on all vertices. B leaves d isolated and contains a triangle. C is disconnected. D retains the triangle and is cyclic.

options.text: {ab,bc,cd}
{ab,bc,ca}
{ab,cd}
{ab,bc,ca,cd}

q_tree_spanning_02.title: Spanning trees after attaching a leaf to a cycle
q_tree_spanning_02.statement: Add a new vertex w to the undirected simple cycle C₆ on v₁,…,v₆ and only the edge v₁w. Count spanning trees of the new graph and identify the edges present in every one.
q_tree_spanning_02.answer_text: There are 6 spanning trees. The bridge v₁w is mandatory. To make the remaining 6-cycle connected and acyclic, delete exactly one of its 6 edges, giving 6 choices. The only common edge is v₁w, since any cycle edge can be the deleted one.
q_tree_spanning_02.explanation: The new graph has 7 vertices, so each spanning tree needs 6 edges. After the mandatory leaf edge, choose 5 from the cycle.
q_tree_spanning_02.grading_criteria: Explain the mandatory bridge: 30%; exhaustive count of 6 choices: 45%; only the leaf edge is common to all: 25%.

q_tree_spanning_03.title: Spanning trees and shortest paths
q_tree_spanning_03.statement: For finite connected undirected simple graphs, which statements are correct? Distances are edge counts.
q_tree_spanning_03.explanation: A is true because BFS records parent edges by shortest-distance layers. B is false: in a triangle, the tree a−b−c has a-to-c distance 2 instead of the original distance 1 via ac. C is true: the unique tree path between the new edge’s endpoints forms exactly one cycle with it. D is false because deleting a cycle edge preserves connectivity.

options.text: A BFS spanning tree rooted at s preserves all unweighted shortest distances from s.
Every spanning tree preserves all original pairwise shortest distances.
Adding an original nontree edge to a spanning tree creates exactly one cycle.
Deleting any edge from the original graph disconnects it.

q_tree_spanning_04.title: Existence of spanning trees and mandatory bridges
q_tree_spanning_04.statement: Prove that every nonempty finite connected undirected simple graph has a spanning tree and that each original bridge lies in every spanning tree.
q_tree_spanning_04.answer_text: If the graph has a cycle, delete one cycle edge. The remaining cycle still connects its endpoints, so the graph stays connected. Repeat: the finite edge count strictly decreases until a connected acyclic graph remains. No vertices were deleted, so this is a spanning tree. Now let e be an original bridge. A spanning tree omitting e would be a connected spanning subgraph of G−e, making all vertices connected there, a contradiction. Thus every bridge lies in every spanning tree.
q_tree_spanning_04.explanation: The construction must preserve all vertices and connectivity. The bridge statement concerns every tree, so rule out any spanning tree that omits it.
q_tree_spanning_04.grading_criteria: Deleting a cycle edge preserves connectivity: 30%; finite termination and spanning-tree conclusion: 25%; bridges in every spanning tree: 45%.

q_tree_spanning_05.title: Comparing BFS and DFS spanning trees
q_tree_spanning_05.statement: An undirected simple graph has vertices {a,b,c,d,e}, edges {ab,ac,bd,cd,ce,de}. Start each search at a and process neighbors alphabetically; DFS is recursive and immediately explores a new neighbor. (1) Give the parent edges recorded by BFS and DFS. (2) Compare their tree distances from a to e.
q_tree_spanning_05.answer_text: BFS records {ab,ac,bd,ce}: discover b,c first, d from b, and e from c. DFS records {ab,bd,dc,ce}, following a→b→d→c→e. The BFS tree distance along a−c−e is 2, also the original shortest distance. The DFS tree distance along a−b−d−c−e is 4.
q_tree_spanning_05.explanation: Undirected cd and dc denote the same edge. Edges to visited vertices must not be recorded as new parent edges.
q_tree_spanning_05.grading_criteria: Each parent-edge set: 30%; both distances and BFS shortest-distance property: 40%.

q_tree_spanning_06.title: Which fundamental-cycle edges can be exchanged?
q_tree_spanning_06.statement: A spanning tree T has vertices {a,b,c,d,e,f} and edges {ab,bc,cd,de,cf}. Add nontree edge ae. Give the fundamental cycle and all original tree edges whose deletion still yields a spanning tree. Explain why cf cannot be deleted.
q_tree_spanning_06.answer_text: The fundamental cycle is a−b−c−d−e−a. Exactly ab,bc,cd,de may be deleted. Deleting any cycle edge leaves a connected acyclic graph. Edge cf is outside the cycle: deleting it isolates f while retaining the original fundamental cycle, so the result is not a spanning tree.
q_tree_spanning_06.explanation: A nontree edge produces only the cycle formed with the original unique path between its endpoints. The removed tree edge cannot be chosen arbitrarily.
q_tree_spanning_06.grading_criteria: Fundamental cycle: 30%; complete set of removable edges: 40%; explain disconnection and a retained cycle after deleting cf: 30%.

q_tree_spanning_07.title: Counting two cycles joined by bridges
q_tree_spanning_07.statement: Initially disjoint triangle a−b−c−a and 4-cycle d−e−f−g−d are joined by cd. Attach a new leaf h to g using gh. Find the spanning-tree count and every mandatory edge.
q_tree_spanning_07.answer_text: Edges cd,gh are bridges and belong to every spanning tree. Delete one of 3 triangle edges and one of 4 square edges independently, giving 3·4=12 spanning trees. Every cycle edge can be omitted in a corresponding choice, so cd,gh are the only mandatory edges.
q_tree_spanning_07.explanation: The graph has 8 vertices. The chosen 2 bridges,2 triangle edges,3 square edges total 7, as required for a spanning tree.
q_tree_spanning_07.grading_criteria: Bridges and their necessity: 30%; independent choices and count 12: 45%; no other mandatory edge and edge-count check: 25%.

q_tree_spanning_08.title: How many deletions produce a spanning forest?
q_tree_spanning_08.statement: A finite undirected simple graph has n vertices,m edges,c components. Retain all vertices and keep each original component connected while deleting every cycle. Prove that exactly m−n+c edges must be deleted.
q_tree_spanning_08.answer_text: Any valid result is a spanning forest of c trees, with n−c remaining edges. Thus m−(n−c)=m−n+c deletions are necessary. Conversely, choose a spanning tree in each original component and retain their union. This is a valid spanning forest deleting exactly that many edges, so the bound is attained. An isolated vertex is a one-vertex tree contributing 0 edges and does not affect the formula.
q_tree_spanning_08.explanation: Original components may not be split, so the result still has exactly c components. Deleting all edges cannot evade this connectivity requirement.
q_tree_spanning_08.grading_criteria: Necessary deletion count: 40%; componentwise construction attaining it: 40%; component constraint and isolated vertices: 20%.

q_tree_mst_01.title: Negative weights do not prevent an MST
q_tree_mst_01.statement: An undirected simple triangle on a,b,c has w(ab)=−3,w(ac)=1,w(bc)=4. What is its MST total weight?
q_tree_mst_01.explanation: A spanning tree chooses any two of the three edges. The possible totals are −2,1,5, with minimum −2 at {ab,ac}. Negative weights are allowed in MSTs.

q_tree_mst_02.title: Kruskal selection and uniqueness
q_tree_mst_02.statement: A connected undirected simple graph on {a,b,c,d} has weights ab:1,ac:4,ad:6,bc:2,bd:5,cd:3. Use Kruskal to find an MST, its edge-addition order and total weight, and decide uniqueness.
q_tree_mst_02.answer_text: Process ab,bc,cd,ac,bd,ad by weight. The first three ab,bc,cd create no cycle. They connect all 4 vertices with 3 edges, so the algorithm stops with total 1+2+3=6. All edge weights are distinct, so the MST is unique.
q_tree_mst_02.explanation: Check for a cycle when adding each edge, rather than merely taking a lightest incident edge at a vertex. Here the first three already form a tree.
q_tree_mst_02.grading_criteria: Correct addition order and tree: 45%; total weight 6: 25%; uniqueness justified by distinct weights: 30%.

q_tree_mst_03.title: Uniqueness and the cut and cycle properties
q_tree_mst_03.statement: Which statements are correct for finite connected undirected simple graphs with real edge weights?
q_tree_mst_03.explanation: A is false: a triangle weighted 1,1,2 still has a unique MST. B is the distinct-weight uniqueness theorem. C follows by exchange: an optimum omitting the unique lightest cut edge can replace another cut edge by it and strictly decrease weight. D is false: a unique heaviest cycle edge belongs to no MST.
q_tree_mst_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for exactly B,C. Note the “unique” condition in C and D.

options.text: If two edge weights agree, the MST is nonunique.
Distinct edge weights guarantee a unique MST.
A unique lightest edge of a cut belongs to every MST.
A unique heaviest edge of a cycle belongs to every MST.

q_tree_mst_04.title: Proving a unique lightest cut edge is mandatory
q_tree_mst_04.statement: Let G be a finite connected undirected weighted simple graph, S a nonempty proper vertex subset, and e the unique lightest edge of δ(S). Prove every MST contains e. If lightest edges tie, must a specified lightest edge still belong to every optimum tree?
q_tree_mst_04.answer_text: Suppose an MST T omits e. Adding e creates a unique cycle. The tree path between its endpoints crosses from S to its complement and contains another cut edge f. Unique lightness gives w(f)>w(e). Deleting f restores a spanning tree with weight w(T)+w(e)−w(f)<w(T), contradicting optimality. Thus every MST contains e. With ties, the claim fails: in a triangle with all weights 1, any two edges form an MST, and any specified edge can be omitted.
q_tree_mst_04.explanation: The strict inequality requires a unique lightest edge. With ties, exchange guarantees some MST contains the edge, not that every MST does.
q_tree_mst_04.grading_criteria: Add an edge to form a cycle and find another cut edge: 35%; strict weight reduction, contradiction, and conclusion: 40%; counterexample for tied lightest edges: 25%.

q_tree_mst_05.title: Prim may choose a heavier edge before a lighter one
q_tree_mst_05.statement: An undirected simple graph on {a,b,c,d,e} has weights ab:7,ac:4,bc:2,bd:5,cd:1,ce:6,de:3,ae:9. Run Prim from a. Give the edge-addition order and total weight, and explain why the first step does not choose the globally lightest edge cd.
q_tree_mst_05.answer_text: Initially the chosen side is {a}; candidates are ab,ac,ae, so choose ac(4). From {a,c}, choose cd(1); from {a,c,d}, choose cb(2); finally choose de(3). The order is ac,cd,cb,de with total 4+1+2+3=10. Initially both endpoints of cd lie outside the chosen set, so it does not cross the current cut and cannot be chosen.
q_tree_mst_05.explanation: Prim compares current cut edges; its chosen weights need not be monotone. Here weight 4 is followed by 1, unlike Kruskal’s global sorting.
q_tree_mst_05.grading_criteria: Four valid cut-edge choices: 60%; total 10: 20%; why cd is initially unavailable: 20%.

q_tree_mst_06.title: A tied lightest edge need not be mandatory
q_tree_mst_06.statement: A triangle has weights ab:1,ac:2,bc:2. List every MST and use δ({c}) to diagnose the assertion that every lightest cut edge belongs to every MST.
q_tree_mst_06.answer_text: The three spanning-tree weights are w({ab,ac})=3,w({ab,bc})=3,w({ac,bc})=4, so exactly the first two are MSTs. In δ({c}), ac,bc tie for lightest, but the first tree omits bc and the second omits ac. A tied lightest edge can be chosen safely but is not mandatory in every optimum. Only unique lightness implies that stronger conclusion.
q_tree_mst_06.explanation: Enumerating all three two-edge subsets establishes both the minimum and all optima. Constructing one optimum alone cannot prove uniqueness.
q_tree_mst_06.grading_criteria: List exactly two MSTs and rule out the third: 50%; identify the cut and tie: 25%; distinguish the logical strengths of the conclusions: 25%.

q_tree_mst_07.title: Excluding a diagonal by the cycle property and counting optima
q_tree_mst_07.statement: All 4 edges of a−b−c−d−a have weight 2. The diagonal ac has weight 5. Find the MST total weight and number of distinct optimum trees, and decide whether the diagonal can belong to one.
q_tree_mst_07.answer_text: Each tree has 3 edges, each of weight at least 2, so its total is at least 6. Deleting any one square edge and retaining the other three attains 6, giving 4 trees. A tree containing ac costs at least 5+2+2=9 and is not optimal. Alternatively ac is the unique heaviest edge in triangle a−b−c−a, so the cycle property excludes it. Thus the minimum is 6 and there are exactly 4 MSTs.
q_tree_mst_07.explanation: An optimum attaining the lower bound uses only weight-2 cycle edges. Every choice of 3 of the 4 forms a path, making the count exhaustive.
q_tree_mst_07.grading_criteria: Lower bound and attainment: 40%; exhaustive count 4: 35%; exclude the diagonal: 25%.

q_tree_mst_08.title: An MST need not give shortest paths
q_tree_mst_08.statement: An undirected simple triangle on s,a,b has weights sa:2,ab:2,sb:3. (1) Find its MST. (2) Find a shortest-path tree rooted at s. Compare total weights and tree distances from s to b, and explain the objectives.
q_tree_mst_08.answer_text: The MST is {sa,ab}, with total weight 4 and tree distance s-to-b of 4. In the original graph, sb has weight 3, less than the cost 4 via a, so the shortest-path tree from s is {sa,sb}, with total weight 5 and s-to-b distance 3. An MST minimizes the whole tree’s total weight; a shortest-path tree preserves each source-to-vertex shortest distance. These are different objectives.
q_tree_mst_08.explanation: Lower MST total weight does not imply each of its root paths is shorter.
q_tree_mst_08.grading_criteria: Both trees and their total weights: 50%; both s-to-b distances: 25%; accurately distinguish objectives: 25%.

q_tree_matrix_tree_01.title: A principal cofactor for a triangle
q_tree_matrix_tree_01.statement: The Laplacian of K₃ is [[2,−1,−1],[−1,2,−1],[−1,−1,2]]. By the matrix-tree theorem, how many spanning trees does it have?
q_tree_matrix_tree_01.explanation: Delete row and column 3 to get [[2,−1],[−1,2]], with determinant 2·2−(−1)(−1)=3. The full matrix has determinant 0, but that is not the requested count.

q_tree_matrix_tree_02.title: Spanning trees of a square with a diagonal
q_tree_matrix_tree_02.statement: An undirected simple graph has vertex order a,b,c,d and edges {ab,bc,cd,da,ac}. Write its Laplacian, delete d’s row and column, and use the matrix-tree theorem to count spanning trees.
q_tree_matrix_tree_02.answer_text: The Laplacian is [[3,−1,−1,−1],[−1,2,−1,0],[−1,−1,3,−1],[−1,0,−1,2]]. Deleting the last row and column gives B=[[3,−1,−1],[−1,2,−1],[−1,−1,3]]. Expanding in its first row, det B=3(6−1)−(−1)(−3−1)+(−1)(1+2)=15−4−3=8. Thus there are 8 spanning trees.
q_tree_matrix_tree_02.explanation: Vertices a,c have degree 3 and b,d have degree 2, giving diagonal 3,2,3,2. The nonadjacent b,d entries must be 0.
q_tree_matrix_tree_02.grading_criteria: Full Laplacian: 35%; correct principal minor: 20%; determinant calculation and result 8: 45%.

q_tree_matrix_tree_03.title: Signs of principal and ordinary minors
q_tree_matrix_tree_03.statement: For a finite undirected simple graph on at least 2 vertices with Laplacian L, which statements are correct?
q_tree_matrix_tree_03.explanation: A is false: L has zero row sums, so even a connected graph has det L=0. B is the matrix-tree theorem. C is true because disconnected graphs have no spanning trees and hence zero principal cofactors. D is false: for K₂, deleting row 1 and column 2 leaves [−1], an ordinary minor −1; multiplying by the cofactor sign gives 1.
q_tree_matrix_tree_03.grading_criteria: Full credit for exactly B,C. Distinguish the determinant of an ordinary minor from its signed cofactor.

options.text: The spanning-tree count of a connected graph is the full det L.
Deleting a matching row and column at different index choices gives equal principal cofactors.
All principal cofactors of order n−1 vanish for a disconnected graph.
Deleting any row and any column always gives an ordinary-minor determinant directly equal to the tree count.

q_tree_matrix_tree_04.title: Adding a leaf preserves the spanning-tree count
q_tree_matrix_tree_04.statement: Let G be a nonempty finite connected undirected simple graph. Attach a new leaf w to an original vertex v by the only new edge vw, obtaining G′. First prove τ(G′)=τ(G) by a spanning-tree correspondence, then explain using principal cofactors.
q_tree_matrix_tree_04.answer_text: Every spanning tree of G′ contains vw, since w has no other incident edge. Removing w,vw gives exactly a spanning tree of G. Conversely, adding w,vw to any spanning tree of G gives one of G′. These inverse operations are a bijection, so the counts agree. For matrices, delete v’s row and column in both graphs. The old-vertex block of G′ is the same as G’s principal minor, and w contributes an independent diagonal block [1]. Thus det L′⁽ᵛ⁾=det L⁽ᵛ⁾·1, giving the same conclusion by the matrix-tree theorem. For single-vertex G, the empty-determinant convention 1 also applies.
q_tree_matrix_tree_04.explanation: Delete the attachment vertex v, removing its degree change and leaving the new leaf in an independent 1×1 block.
q_tree_matrix_tree_04.grading_criteria: Bijection between spanning trees: 45%; choose the deletion index and explain blocks: 35%; determinant and boundary case: 20%.

q_tree_matrix_tree_05.title: Constructing the Laplacian of a path
q_tree_matrix_tree_05.statement: For the undirected simple path a−b−c−d in order a,b,c,d, write its Laplacian L and check every row sum.
q_tree_matrix_tree_05.explanation: Endpoints have degree 1 and internal vertices degree 2. Off-diagonal entries are −1 for adjacency and 0 otherwise. Zero row sums also help catch sign errors.
q_tree_matrix_tree_05.grading_criteria: Four diagonal degrees: 30%; off-diagonal entries and symmetry: 45%; check each row: 25%.

q_tree_matrix_tree_06.title: Why a disconnected graph has a zero cofactor
q_tree_matrix_tree_06.statement: G has only edges ab,cd and vertex order a,b,c,d. Write its Laplacian, delete d’s row and column, compute the determinant, and relate it to spanning-tree existence.
q_tree_matrix_tree_06.answer_text: L=[[1,−1,0,0],[−1,1,0,0],[0,0,1,−1],[0,0,−1,1]]. Deleting the last row and column gives B=[[1,−1,0],[−1,1,0],[0,0,1]], so det B=(1−1)·1=0. The graph has two components and cannot have a spanning tree connecting all vertices. Its tree count is 0, agreeing with the determinant.
q_tree_matrix_tree_06.explanation: The argument does not use merely the fact that every full Laplacian determinant vanishes. It computes the correct principal cofactor, whose zero value reflects disconnection.
q_tree_matrix_tree_06.grading_criteria: L and principal minor: 45%; determinant 0: 25%; explain disconnection and no spanning tree: 30%.

q_tree_matrix_tree_07.title: Two triangles sharing a vertex
q_tree_matrix_tree_07.statement: An undirected simple graph has edges {ab,bc,ca,cd,de,ec}: two triangles sharing only c and no other edges. Delete c’s Laplacian row and column and use blocks to count spanning trees.
q_tree_matrix_tree_07.answer_text: Order the remaining vertices a,b,d,e. The principal minor is [[2,−1,0,0],[−1,2,0,0],[0,0,2,−1],[0,0,−1,2]], with two identical 2×2 diagonal blocks. Each has determinant 4−1=3, so the full determinant is 3·3=9, giving 9 spanning trees.
q_tree_matrix_tree_07.explanation: Alternatively, delete one edge independently from each triangle, giving 3·3 choices. The shared vertex c is not an additional edge or vertex to be selected.
q_tree_matrix_tree_07.grading_criteria: Correct block principal minor: 45%; both block determinants and product 9: 35%; explain independent decomposition: 20%.

q_tree_matrix_tree_08.title: A formula for spanning trees of complete graphs
q_tree_matrix_tree_08.statement: Let n≥2. Given det(aIₖ+bJₖ)=a^(k−1)(a+kb), where Iₖ is the identity and Jₖ the all-ones matrix, use the matrix-tree theorem to derive the spanning-tree count of Kₙ and evaluate it at n=4.
q_tree_matrix_tree_08.answer_text: Each Kₙ vertex has degree n−1 and every off-diagonal Laplacian entry is −1, so L=nIₙ−Jₙ. Delete any row and the matching column to get B=nIₙ₋₁−Jₙ₋₁. Substitute k=n−1,a=n,b=−1 in the given formula: det B=n^(n−2)[n−(n−1)]=n^(n−2). Hence τ(Kₙ)=n^(n−2); for n=4 this is 4²=16.
q_tree_matrix_tree_08.explanation: The cofactor has size n−1 but is still nI−J, not (n−1)I−J, which would give incorrect diagonal degrees.
q_tree_matrix_tree_08.grading_criteria: Full L and principal-minor forms: 40%; correct substitution into the determinant formula: 35%; general formula and 16: 25%.

q_graph_domination_09.title: Constructing a minimum edge cover from a matching
q_graph_domination_09.statement: For the undirected simple path P₅=1−2−3−4−5, find maximum matching number ν(P₅), minimum edge-cover number ρ(P₅), and a minimum edge cover. If a new isolated vertex z with no incident edges is added, does an edge cover still exist? Write an edge cover as an edge set.
q_graph_domination_09.answer_text: ν(P₅)=2, for example M={12,34}; 5 vertices cannot support 3 edges with disjoint endpoints. The graph has no isolated vertices, so ρ=5−2=3. Add 45 to M to get minimum edge cover F={12,34,45}, covering all 5 vertices. Two edges cover at most 4 vertices, directly confirming at least 3 are needed. After adding isolated z, no edge cover exists: no selectable edge has z as an endpoint.
q_graph_domination_09.explanation: The shared endpoint of 34,45 is allowed in an edge cover; it only prevents them from forming a matching. The formula requires no isolated vertices and cannot be mechanically applied to the new graph as 6−2.
